questions.question: You're in Villahermosa, by the river named after a Spanish explorer who sailed it in 1518, a year before Cortés. Who was he?
hints: He was sent from Cuba to explore the Gulf coast.
He was a relative of the governor of Cuba.
His river forms a large basin together with the Usumacinta.
questions.fun_fact: When Grijalva's expedition returned to Cuba with gold, it encouraged the planning of Hernán Cortés's expedition.

media.credit: Alfonsobouchot · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alfonsobouchot

questions.description: A colonial factory where nobody was eager to clock in for the day.
questions.question: New Spain had obrajes (workshops) in Puebla, Querétaro and Texcoco, where workers sometimes lived locked in. What did they make?
hints: What they made was sold across the viceroyalty, and people used it every day.
Centuries later, Puebla and Querétaro were still famous for factories in that same industry.
Its raw material came from sheep.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its obrajes, Querétaro became one of the great textile centers of New Spain.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: The Mexica throne was fought over harder than the last pan dulce in the basket.
questions.question: After meeting Cortés in 1519, Moctezuma ended up a prisoner of the Spanish. Who ruled the Mexica right after him?
hints: He was Moctezuma's brother.
He ruled for a very short time, just a few months.
He led the Mexica on the Noche Triste.
questions.fun_fact: Cuitláhuac ruled for about 80 days before dying of smallpox, a disease brought by the Europeans.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: Words that arrived before Cortés and decided to stay for good.
questions.question: Which of these words for places does NOT come from Nahuatl?
hints: Three of them were used in the Valley of Mexico.
The odd one out comes from another Indigenous language, spoken far from the Valley of Mexico.
It comes from a language of the Yucatán Peninsula.
questions.fun_fact: “Tianguis” comes from the Nahuatl “tianquiztli”, which means market.

media.credit: Unnamed Nahua contributors under leadership of Bernardino de Sahagún · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unnamed Nahua contributors under leadership of Bernardino de Sahagún

questions.description: Before leaving for California, this friar left behind facades more decorated than a wedding cake.
questions.question: Fray Junípero Serra built this mission in the Sierra Gorda before leaving for California. In which Mexican state is it?
hints: It is one of five Franciscan missions that are World Heritage Sites.
The town where it stands bears the friar's surname.
The capital of that state has a famous aqueduct.
questions.fun_fact: The mission's town is called Jalpan de Serra in honor of the friar, who was born on the island of Mallorca.

media.credit: Danicalzadar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Danicalzadar

questions.description: A top so pretty you'd feel bad wearing it to eat pozole.
questions.question: At a market in Oaxaca, you try on an embroidered blouse made of manta. What fiber is manta made of?
hints: It's a plant fiber that doesn't come from any animal.
The plant grows fluffy white puffs.
Most T-shirts are made of the same fiber.
questions.fun_fact: Manta is unbleached cotton cloth, which is why it has that typical off-white color.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: A cloth so humble it ended up as one of the most famous in Mexico.
questions.question: This cloth is woven from ixtle, the fiber of the maguey. It was used to carry things, and the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared on Juan Diego's. What is it called?
hints: It's a rough, scratchy cloth, nothing like silk.
Juan Diego's is also called a “tilma”.
Its name starts with “aya…”.
questions.fun_fact: The original image of the Virgin of Guadalupe is kept in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

media.credit: Marc Ryckaert (MJJR) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Marc Ryckaert (MJJR)

questions.description: A town in Puebla where December starts halfway through the year.
questions.question: Chignahuapan, Puebla, makes millions of Christmas ornament balls by hand and holds a fair just for them. What are they made of?
hints: You have to handle them very carefully.
They shine brightly and light passes through them.
They're shaped by blowing, and if they fall on the floor they shatter.
questions.fun_fact: In Chignahuapan the ornaments are painted by hand, and many carry whatever name the customer asks for.

media.credit: Hullian111 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hullian111

questions.description: A toy that decides whether today you're a candy millionaire or left with nothing.
questions.question: You spin it on the table. It has six sides that say things like “toma todo” (take all) or “todos ponen” (everyone pays). What is it called?
hints: It's played in a group, betting candy or beans.
You spin it with two fingers, with no string.
Its name starts with “piri…”.
questions.fun_fact: Similar toys exist in other parts of the world, like the dreidel played at Hanukkah.

media.credit: Keizers · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Keizers

questions.description: A skirt that spins so much it makes the charro dizzy.
questions.question: The Jalisco dress has a wide skirt and colorful ribbons, and it's worn to dance the jarabe tapatío. What does “tapatío” mean?
hints: It's a word for where someone comes from.
It refers to a city.
It's the capital of Jalisco.
questions.fun_fact: The jarabe tapatío is so famous that outside Mexico many people know it as the “Mexican hat dance.”

media.credit: Mike.isilra · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mike.isilra

questions.description: A vocho that dressed up for a gala and never drove again.
questions.question: The Vochol is a vocho (VW Beetle) covered in glass beads by artisans of a people who call themselves Wixárika. What is their other name?
hints: They live in the mountains where Jalisco, Nayarit, Zacatecas and Durango meet.
They are famous for their yarn art and beadwork.
They hold peyote and the deer sacred.
questions.fun_fact: The Vochol, from 2010, has more than 2 million beads glued on by hand.

media.credit: Albarubescens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Albarubescens

questions.description: A bag that the rancher and his horse share without a fight.
questions.question: On ranches, the morral isn't only carried on the shoulder: it also goes over the horse's head. What for?
wrong_answers: To shade it from the sun
hints: The horse loves this moment.
There's something inside it.
It holds oats or corn.
questions.fun_fact: The first meaning of “morral” in the Spanish dictionary is exactly that bag of food hung from an animal's head.

media.credit: Carl Young · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carl Young

questions.description: A market so punctual it only shows up for work one day a week.
questions.question: Every Saturday, Mexico City hosts the Bazar Sábado, famous for its crafts and painters. In which neighborhood?
hints: It's in the south of the city, with cobblestone streets.
It's held on Plaza San Jacinto.
It's home to the house-studio of Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo.
questions.fun_fact: While the bazaar fills an old mansion, painters show their canvases outside on the plaza.

media.credit: Bluerasberry · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bluerasberry

questions.description: Three cousins who came out of the kiln, and one who crashed the family reunion.
questions.question: Which of these Mexican crafts is NOT made of clay?
hints: One of them comes from Guerrero.
That one never goes into the potter's kiln.
It is made on wood or gourds.
questions.fun_fact: Olinalá lacquerware is traditionally made on linaloe wood, from a very fragrant tree.

media.credit: Bluerasberry · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bluerasberry

questions.description: Because even in the afterlife you crave something cool to drink after such a long trip.
questions.question: Many ofrendas include the departed person's favorite drink, such as pulque. Which plant does pulque come from?
hints: It's a big plant with thick leaves and spines along the edges.
Its sweet sap, before it ferments, is called aguamiel.
It's a close relative of the agave used for tequila.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Spanish arrived, pulque was a sacred drink that almost only elders, priests and people at ceremonies were allowed to drink.

media.credit: NPS Photo · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NPS Photo

questions.description: A four-year trip with no layovers, no luggage and no Wi-Fi.
questions.question: For the Mexica, people who died a natural death traveled for four years through nine levels, guided by a dog. Where did they end up?
hints: It was a dark, cold place under the earth.
Warriors and people who drowned didn't go there, only those who died of old age or illness.
Its lord was Mictlantecuhtli, the god of death.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the xoloitzcuintle dog helped the soul cross a raging river on one of the levels of the journey.

media.credit: Canarian · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Canarian

questions.description: Some dreams are forgotten when you wake up, and others end up parading down Reforma.
questions.question: Every October, the Monumental Alebrijes Parade moves through Mexico City. Which cartonero invented alebrijes after dreaming of them?
hints: He was a Mexico City craftsman who made papier-mâché Judas figures and piñatas.
He had that dream in 1936, while he was very sick.
His first name was Pedro.
questions.fun_fact: As he told it himself, in his dream some fantastic creatures shouted a single word: “Alebrijes!”

media.credit: Salcedo95 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Salcedo95

questions.description: A very elegant lady who hasn't eaten in over a century.
questions.question: Every year, Aguascalientes holds the Festival de Calaveras to honor the creator of this engraving, who was born in that city. Who was he?
hints: He was an engraver who worked for Mexico City newspapers in the late 19th century.
He didn't call her Catrina, but “La Calavera Garbancera.”
His initials are J. G. P.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Catrina” came from Diego Rivera, who painted her in his mural “Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central.”

media.credit: Arsacio Vanegas · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arsacio Vanegas

questions.description: On November 2, the whole family packs up flowers, food and even the guitar, and nobody stays home.
questions.question: In Mexico, when someone says “el 2 de noviembre vamos al panteón,” where are they going?
hints: On that day, many families spend hours there with food and music.
Families bring cempasúchil flowers.
It's where the dead are buried.
questions.fun_fact: The word “panteón” comes from Greek and means “of all the gods”: it was the name of a temple in ancient Rome.

media.credit: Joydeep · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joydeep

questions.description: Works the night shift, never complains and brings its own glass.
questions.question: In Mexico, what is this candle in a glass jar called, the kind placed on ofrendas and altars?
hints: You can buy it at the corner store or at the market.
It can stay lit for several days in a row.
Its name comes from the Spanish «velar», to keep watch over someone at night.
questions.fun_fact: The glass shields the flame from the wind, which is why veladoras stay lit all night in the cemetery.

media.credit: Pittigrilli · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pittigrilli

questions.description: A family tree with more branches than a bunch of cempasúchil marigolds.
questions.question: In the movie Coco, which of these characters is NOT related to Mamá Coco?
hints: He is a very famous singer in the movie.
For most of the movie, Miguel thinks he is his great-great-grandfather.
He stole his friend's songs.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Mamá Coco's real name is Socorro.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: They tell the family not to spill the atole, and for good reason.
questions.question: On the ofrenda, a cloth covers the table. It is often embroidered and almost always white. What does that color stand for?
hints: It has to do with the color, not the fabric.
It's the same thing many people link to a bride's white dress.
It means clean, without a stain.
questions.fun_fact: Papel picado, candles, water, salt and pan de muerto usually go on top of the white cloth.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: A drink that leaves your tongue purple, as if you'd been snacking on crayons.
questions.question: At the agua fresca stand there's a dark purple one made with zarzamora. Which group of fruits does zarzamora belong to?
hints: It isn't sour like a lime or hard like a walnut.
It grows on thorny bushes.
Each fruit is a cluster of tiny juicy beads, and the plant is related to the rose.
questions.fun_fact: Michoacán grows the vast majority of Mexico's zarzamoras, and many of them are sold abroad.

media.credit: Gzzz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gzzz

questions.description: It makes abuelita's kitchen smell wonderful before you're even awake.
questions.question: It's sold in rolled-up sticks, smells sweet, and is always in café de olla and arroz con leche. What is it?
hints: It's a brown spice.
It comes from the bark of a tree.
It's also sprinkled on churros with sugar.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries that imports the most cinnamon in the world.

media.credit: Cristina Zapata Pérez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cristina Zapata Pérez

questions.description: Breakfast for people running late, gulped down standing up at the market.
questions.question: I'm a grain sold in flakes. Cooked with milk I become porridge, and at the market they blend me with banana. What am I?
hints: Horses eat a lot of me too.
My flakes are flat and cream-colored.
My name starts with O and has just four letters.
questions.fun_fact: An oat and banana licuado is one of the quickest and cheapest breakfasts at Mexican markets.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: The most Mexican way to drink a soda with no cup and no bottle.
questions.question: It's clear, tied with a rubber band around the straw, and the tiendita hands you your soda to go in it. What is it made of?
hints: The soda doesn't make it soggy or tear it.
That's why it causes so much pollution when it's thrown in the street.
It's the same material as lots of water bottles.
questions.fun_fact: You get your soda in a bag so the tiendita can keep the returnable bottle.

media.author: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada

questions.description: A mountain forest, a crowd of insurgents and a decision people still argue about.
questions.question: In October 1810, the insurgents beat the royalists at Monte de las Cruces, but their leader refused to enter Mexico City. Who was he?
hints: It was just a few weeks after the War of Independence began.
This leader had started the rebellion in a town in Guanajuato.
He is the priest who gave the Grito de Dolores.
questions.fun_fact: The battle took place in a mountain forest between Toluca and Mexico City, at about 3,000 m (9,800 ft) above sea level.

media.credit: Ximesmp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ximesmp

questions.description: Three European powers agreed on a group trip to Veracruz, and it wasn't exactly a vacation.
questions.question: In 1861, Spain, France and Britain signed the Convention of London and sent ships to Veracruz. Which decision by Juárez caused it?
questions.answer: Suspending payments on the foreign debt
wrong_answers: Closing the port of Veracruz to trade
hints: Juárez had just won the Reform War, and the government had no money.
The three countries said a Mexican law from July 1861 was costing them money.
Juárez decreed that they would not be paid for two years.
questions.fun_fact: Spain and Britain pulled out in 1862 after the Treaties of La Soledad; only France stayed and invaded the country.

media.credit: xiquinhosilva · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: xiquinhosilva

questions.description: A state that took a hero's name and ordered spring weather all year round.

hints: Cuernavaca is called “the city of eternal spring.”
The hero it's named after held out in the famous Siege of Cuautla, in this same state.
That priest wore a bandana tied around his head.
questions.fun_fact: Morelos is Mexico's second-smallest state; only Tlaxcala is smaller.

media.credit: Laloixx · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Laloixx

questions.description: A short phrase that fits on a coat of arms, on a wall, and in many hearts.
questions.question: Complete Vicente Guerrero's famous phrase from when he refused to give up the insurgent fight: “La patria es…”
hints: He said it when he was asked to surrender in exchange for a pardon from the viceroy.
He said it to his own father, who had brought him the offer.
It means the opposite of “last.”
questions.fun_fact: As president, Vicente Guerrero decreed the abolition of slavery in Mexico in 1829.

media.credit: Prsjl · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Prsjl

questions.description: Miners in helmets, lots of copper, and zero interest in earning less than the neighbors.
questions.question: In the 1906 Cananea strike, Mexican miners at a copper mine demanded the same pay as American workers. In which state was it?
hints: The mine was very close to the US border.
It's a northwestern state, famous for its desert and its carne asada.
Its capital is Hermosillo.
questions.fun_fact: The miners also demanded an 8-hour workday, a right that was later written into the 1917 Constitution.

media.credit: David Ratledge · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Ratledge

questions.description: Gown, high heels and nerves of steel: welcome to Hollywood's fanciest night.
questions.question: Who was the first Indigenous Mexican woman nominated for the Oscar for Best Actress, for the film “Roma”?
hints: She is from Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca.
Before acting, she trained to be a preschool teacher.
In “Roma” she played Cleo, a live-in housekeeper.
questions.fun_fact: Yalitza had never acted before “Roma” and ended up at the casting almost by chance, thanks to her sister.

media.author: Greg in Hollywood (Greg Hernandez)

questions.description: The original belt: no buckle, no holes, and more colors than a market.
questions.question: The Indigenous faja (sash) wraps several times around the waist, holds up a skirt or trousers, and is woven on a backstrap loom. What fibers is it traditionally made of?
hints: One fiber comes from a plant, the other from an animal.
They're the same fibers as in many sarapes and huipiles.
One grows in a fluffy white boll; the other is sheared from sheep.
questions.fun_fact: On a backstrap loom, the weaver keeps the threads tight with her own body by leaning back.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A language with more embroidery than a Sunday tablecloth.
questions.question: I'm spoken in Hidalgo, Querétaro and the State of Mexico; in the Mezquital Valley I'm called Hñähñu, and Tenango embroidery comes from my people. Which language am I?

My embroidery is full of colorful animals and plants.
Many tourists buy the “Lele” dolls of Querétaro, made by my people.
questions.fun_fact: The Lele doll from Amealco, Querétaro, is made by Otomí women artisans and has become a symbol of the state.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: Democracy with no ballots, no billboards and no catchy campaign jingles.
questions.question: In most municipalities of Oaxaca, people choose their leaders in a community assembly, with no political parties. What is this system called?
hints: It rests on traditions passed down from generation to generation.
Today the law also calls it “indigenous normative systems.”
Its name refers to the practices and habits of each community.
questions.fun_fact: More than 400 of Oaxaca’s 570 municipalities choose their leaders this way.

media.credit: Carlos.morales.valladarez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos.morales.valladarez

questions.description: A relative of the chiles that came out with no personality at all.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this big, fleshy pepper that isn't spicy at all called?
hints: They come in red, yellow, orange and green.
It's almost square, with three or four bumps on the bottom.
It's often used on pizzas and in salads.
questions.fun_fact: The bell pepper is the same species as the jalapeño and the serrano, but it has almost no capsaicin.

media.credit: AntanO · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AntanO

questions.description: A salsa that starts out crunchy and ends in a house fire.
questions.question: Salsa de cacahuate is ground from roasted peanuts, garlic and a thin, dried, bright red, very hot chile. Which one?
hints: It is not a wide or dark chile.
It is small and long, and it's pretty hot.
Its Spanish name sounds like something that grows in a forest.
questions.fun_fact: The word “cacahuate” comes from the Nahuatl “tlalcacahuatl,” meaning “earth cacao.”

media.credit: Chandapiwa Malema · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chandapiwa Malema

questions.description: A red fruit crossed the ocean, and then Europe showed it off as its own.
questions.question: The Mexica called it xitomatl, and the Spanish took it to Europe. In which century was that?
hints: It reached Europe long before it became a common ingredient in Italian cooking.
It happened at the time of the Spanish conquest of the Mexica.
It's the same century Shakespeare was born in.
questions.fun_fact: At first, many Europeans thought the tomato was poisonous and grew it only as a decorative plant.

media.credit: Rosemania · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rosemania

questions.description: The art of saying “Can you do it for less?” with a face like you're about to leave.
questions.question: You ask for “una rebajita” and haggle over the price. Where is haggling NOT usually done?
hints: In one place, the price is printed on labels.
There you pay at a cash register.
There you push a cart down the aisles.
questions.fun_fact: “Tianguis” comes from the Nahuatl word “tianquiztli”, which means market.

media.credit: Rjcastillo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rjcastillo

questions.description: What the squash hides inside and you snack on in the park.
questions.question: They're squash seeds: toasted with salt and lime, sold in little bags, and ground for pipián. What are they called?
hints: They're green inside and flat.
You eat them one by one, as a snack.
Their name means “little seeds” in Spanish.
questions.fun_fact: Pipián is a mole thickened with ground squash seeds.

media.credit: Jocelyn Maloney jocelyn · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jocelyn Maloney jocelyn

questions.description: A tiny seed that matters a lot, whatever the saying claims.
questions.question: It's a long brown seed with a strong smell, used in adobos and birria, and people say “me importa un…”. Which spice is it?
hints: It's used whole or ground.
It smells strong and a bit earthy.
It's part of a Spanish saying for not caring about something at all.
questions.fun_fact: Cumin came to Mexico with the Spanish: it's from the Mediterranean and the Middle East.

media.credit: Carloscurielfotografo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carloscurielfotografo

questions.description: They've been standing guard for more than a thousand years and haven't asked for a bathroom break once.
questions.question: These giant warrior statues stand in Tula, Hidalgo. Which people carved them?
hints: They lived before the Aztecs.
Tula was the capital of their kingdom.
The Aztecs admired them so much that they used their name to mean “great artist.”
questions.fun_fact: The Atlantes are about 4.6 m (15 ft) tall and once held up the roof of a temple.

media.credit: Rafael Aparicio · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rafael Aparicio

questions.description: A neighborhood with so much attitude that even boxing gloves get nervous walking in.
questions.question: It's in central Mexico City, people call it “el barrio bravo,” and boxing champions came from there. What is Tepito most famous for?

They say you can find everything there, from clothes to gadgets.
questions.fun_fact: Its name is thought to come from the Nahuatl “teocalli tepiton,” meaning “small temple.”

media.credit: Carlos Pacheco · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Pacheco

questions.description: A monument so devoted to its hero that for decades it kept something very personal of his.
questions.question: The Monument to Álvaro Obregón in San Ángel honors the president from 1920 to 1924. Who succeeded him as president?
hints: Like Obregón, he came from Sonora.
He founded the party that, over the years, became the PRI.
The years when he kept ruling from behind the scenes were called “the Maximato.”
questions.fun_fact: Until 1989, the arm Obregón lost in a 1915 battle was displayed inside the monument, kept in a jar.

media.credit: Anacrisq92 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Anacrisq92

questions.description: A boat ride with no sea, no waves and no seasickness.
questions.question: The Paseo Santa Lucía is a man-made river in Monterrey where boats take people for rides. About how long is it?

media.author: México en Fotos, A.C.

questions.description: A museum where not touching things is against the rules.
questions.question: The most famous children's museum in Mexico City is called Papalote. What is a papalote?
questions.answer: A toy that flies in the wind on a string

A wooden puppet worked with strings
A little boat made out of paper

It works best on a very windy day.
In Spain and Colombia it's called a cometa.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Nahuatl “papálotl,” which means butterfly.

media.credit: Robertson G. Adams · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robertson G. Adams

questions.description: A pyramid hidden in the jungle, perfect for a giant game of hide-and-seek.
questions.question: This is Nohoch Mul, the tallest pyramid at the Maya site of Cobá. Which Mexican state is it in?

media.author: Ken Thomas

questions.description: A place where the loudest shouts don't come from the crowd, but from the ropes.
questions.question: It's in Colonia Doctores, opened in 1956 and is home to the oldest company of its sport in the world. Arena México is “the Cathedral” of which sport?

There are rudos and técnicos.
Many of its idols hide their faces behind a mask.
questions.fun_fact: The company that uses it, CMLL, was founded in 1933 and is the oldest of its kind in the world still running.

media.credit: Ian T. McFarland from Los Angeles, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ian T. McFarland from Los Angeles, USA

questions.description: It shows up at the beach every summer with no reservation, and nobody invited it.
questions.question: This brown seaweed covers the beaches of the Mexican Caribbean every year. When it rots on the sand, what does it smell like?
hints: The smell comes from a gas given off as it rots.
That gas contains sulfur.
Think of a breakfast left out of the fridge and forgotten for days.
questions.fun_fact: Sargassum floats thanks to little air-filled bubbles that look like tiny grapes.

media.credit: Clump · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Clump

questions.description: People who dance La Bamba even in the tortilla line.
questions.question: What do you call the people from the port of Veracruz?
hints: Not the people from Mexico City, and not the ones from Guadalajara.
Their harp and jarana music goes by the same name.
“Son …” is the music of this port.
questions.fun_fact: The port of Veracruz was the first city the Spanish founded in what is now Mexico, in 1519.

media.credit: Burkhard Mücke · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Burkhard Mücke

questions.description: A 30-ton gymnast who comes to Mexico on vacation.
questions.question: Every winter, this whale comes to give birth in a bay shared by Jalisco and Nayarit. What is the bay called?
hints: Its calves are born in warm, calm waters.
The bay is on the Pacific side.
Puerto Vallarta is there.
questions.fun_fact: Male humpback whales sing songs that can last more than ten minutes.

media.credit: Giles Laurent · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Giles Laurent

questions.description: Graffiti artists so ancient that nobody can scold them anymore.
questions.question: The Olmec paintings in the Juxtlahuaca caves, in Guerrero, are among the oldest in Mesoamerica. How old are they?
hints: They are much older than the arrival of the Spanish.
The Olmecs flourished before the Classic Maya and the Mexica.
They date from around 1000 BC.
questions.fun_fact: To see the Juxtlahuaca paintings, you have to walk more than a kilometer (over half a mile) inside the cave.

media.credit: Johnragla · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Johnragla

questions.description: A fish that thinks it's a sailboat, and nobody has the heart to tell it.
questions.question: Every winter, hundreds of sailfish gather off Isla Mujeres. Why do they raise their huge back fin?
hints: It has to do with food.
Several of them do it together, like shepherds.
This way they squeeze their prey into a tight ball.
questions.fun_fact: When it wants to swim really fast, the sailfish folds its fin down and tucks it into a groove along its back.

media.credit: European Space Agency · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: European Space Agency

questions.description: A water staircase you go down with no handrail and a life jacket on.
questions.question: Near Ciudad Valles, in the Huasteca Potosina, a river forms seven waterfalls in a row, and people jump from one to the next. What are they called?
hints: They're not in Chiapas or Chihuahua.
They're several small drops, not one giant one.
Their name is a Spanish word for an animal that climbs trees.
questions.fun_fact: The water in the Huasteca Potosina is turquoise because it carries a lot of dissolved calcium carbonate.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: A traveler who crosses five states and never once asks for a ride.
questions.question: “I'm born in the State of Mexico, cross Querétaro, Guanajuato and Michoacán, and end in Lake Chapala.” Which river am I?
hints: I flow through the center of the country, not along a border.
After leaving Chapala I carry on under another name: the Santiago River.
I share my name with a city near Toluca.
questions.fun_fact: Together, the Lerma and the Santiago form one of the longest river systems in Mexico.

media.credit: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico

questions.description: A tianguis so big that not even the Sunday one in your neighborhood comes close.
questions.question: Hernán Cortés wrote that at the great market of Tlatelolco, on the shore of Lake Texcoco, about how many people gathered every day?
hints: It was the biggest market the Spaniards had ever seen.
It was more than the population of many Spanish cities at the time.
It's a five-digit number.
questions.fun_fact: At the Tlatelolco market, cacao beans were used as money.

media.credit: Luis Alvaz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Alvaz

questions.description: A craft so devilishly good that even el chamuco shows off his portrait.
questions.question: The Purépecha women of Ocumicho, Michoacán, shape colorful little clay devils. According to one village tale, why did they start making them?
questions.answer: So the devil had a place to live and left the village alone
wrong_answers: To win a bet the devil had made with the village
To scare children who didn't obey their parents
To ask the devil to bring rain in the dry season
hints: It has to do with keeping a very mischievous someone calm.
They say the devil used to roam the village freely, playing tricks.
They gave el chamuco his own little clay house so he'd stop bothering people.
questions.fun_fact: Many Ocumicho devils show the devil in everyday scenes: driving, at the doctor's, or even playing soccer.

media.credit: Fernando Hernández Ramírez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fernando Hernández Ramírez

questions.description: The tiniest real estate on the whole peninsula.
questions.question: In Yucatán, some farmers build a little stone house in the middle of their milpa. According to Maya tradition, what is it for?
questions.answer: For an alux to live in and guard the milpa
wrong_answers: To store next year's corn seeds
For souls to rest on Día de Muertos
To offer the first elote to the rain god
hints: Farmers often leave food and drink in the little house.
They believe it's for someone who lives in the milpa all year, not just for one day or season.
It's like a little Maya goblin that needs a home of its own.
questions.fun_fact: They say that if the alux gets no offerings, it turns mischievous: it throws pebbles and scares anyone passing through the milpa.

media.credit: KONTRA.PKC · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: KONTRA.PKC

questions.description: Deer have a lawyer too, and it doesn't charge in pesos.
questions.question: You're hunting in the Yucatán bush and kill more deer than you need. According to the Maya, who will punish you?
hints: It's a guardian of the animals of the wild.
Hunters feared it most, more than farmers did.
They say it looks like a little deer with a wasp nest between its antlers.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional Maya hunters asked it for permission and left it offerings before going out to hunt.

media.credit: USFWS Pacific · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: USFWS Pacific

questions.description: The longest-working model in all of Mexico, and she's never once asked for a raise.
questions.question: Since 1930, a mannequin in a wedding dress in a Chihuahua shop has looked so real that people say she's a person. What is her nickname?
hints: She stands in downtown Chihuahua City.
Her nickname comes from the name of the shop's owner.
It sounds like an affectionate nickname for “Pascuala.”
questions.fun_fact: Some people swear her eyes follow customers around and that her dress is changed behind closed doors.

media.credit: Jwslubbock · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jwslubbock

questions.description: It's called “deer's eye,” but no deer had anything to do with it.
questions.question: Mexican markets sell the “ojo de venado” for hanging on babies. According to tradition, what is it for?
questions.answer: To protect them from the evil eye
wrong_answers: To help their teeth come in painlessly
To help them sleep through the night
To help them learn to walk early
hints: The custom is centuries old, and even some adults wear one.
It's made from a large seed and a red thread.
It works against the “heavy” stares of some adults.
questions.fun_fact: Despite its name, the ojo de venado is the seed of a climbing plant, and it often comes with a tiny saint's picture or a red ribbon.

media.credit: Forest and Kim Starr · CC BY 3.0 us · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Forest and Kim Starr

questions.description: A classic to watch with the lights on and the windows shut tight.
questions.question: A 1968 Mexican horror film by Carlos Enrique Taboada: at a girls' boarding school, students hear voices in a forbidden tower. Which film is it?
hints: It is the most famous of Taboada's horror films.
The students stay at the boarding school during the vacation.
The title says that even something that blows feels fear.
questions.fun_fact: A remake starring Martha Higareda came out in 2007.

media.credit: denisbin from Adelaide, Australia · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: denisbin from Adelaide, Australia

questions.description: A soup that shows up with its own little slice, ready for the photo.
questions.question: This is sopa de lima, a chicken broth with strips of fried tortilla. Which Mexican regional cuisine is it typical of?
hints: It's a cuisine from southeastern Mexico that uses lots of achiote and citrus.
Its region has coasts on both the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico.
It's from the peninsula where Mérida and Chichén Itzá are.
questions.fun_fact: The Yucatán lima isn't just any lime: it has a very fragrant aroma and a taste unlike the common lime.

media.credit: Isaacvp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isaacvp

questions.description: A chapter of Yucatán's history that grade-school textbooks barely mention.
questions.question: Which Maya leader attacked the town of Tepich in July 1847, starting the Caste War of Yucatán?
hints: He was a batab, a Maya chief from eastern Yucatán.
He led the uprising together with Jacinto Pat.
His surname is a Maya word of just three letters.
questions.fun_fact: The Caste War lasted more than 50 years; it is usually said to have ended in 1901, when the army took Chan Santa Cruz.

media.credit: Dave R Chasteen · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dave R Chasteen

questions.description: A sport so old it makes soccer look like the new kid on the block.
questions.question: You're in Sinaloa watching ulama, a game where a heavy rubber ball is hit with the hips. How long has the ballgame been played in Mesoamerica?
hints: It was played long before the Spanish arrived.
The oldest rubber balls come from the Olmecs.
The oldest known court dates from around 1650 BC.
questions.fun_fact: Ulama balls are made of solid rubber and can weigh more than 3 kg (6.6 lb).

media.credit: Wolfgang Sauber · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wolfgang Sauber

questions.description: Four brothers with a really heavy job and no vacation days.
questions.question: The Bacabs were four Maya gods: each lived at a cardinal point, had a color and protected the bees. What did they hold up?
hints: They are shown with their arms raised.
Each one stood at a corner of the world.
Without them, what's above would fall onto the Earth.
questions.fun_fact: Maya beekeepers in Yucatán still raise the melipona bee, which has no stinger.

media.credit: MarvinBikolano · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MarvinBikolano

questions.description: It comes wrapped like a birthday present, but you open it with more hunger than excitement.
questions.question: Look at these tamales. What is their dough made of?
hints: It's the same ingredient as in tortillas.
The Mexica had gods devoted to this plant, such as Centéotl.
It's a tall plant that grows elotes.
questions.fun_fact: The word “tamal” comes from the Nahuatl “tamalli,” which means something like “wrapped.”

media.credit: Nsaum75 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nsaum75

questions.description: The real boss of the taquería table, even though nobody invited it.
questions.question: Look at this taquería green salsa. Besides the chile, what fruit is its base?
hints: It's a small round fruit wrapped in a dry papery husk.
It tastes tart and is picked while still green.
It's a relative of the red tomato.
questions.fun_fact: “Tomato” comes from the Nahuatl “tomatl”, and in Mexico the red tomato is called “jitomate”, from “xictomatl”.

media.credit: Missvain · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Missvain

questions.description: A stone shaped like a temple, for when the real temple won't fit in the room.
questions.question: This Mexica stone monument is shaped like a pyramid with a staircase, with an eagle on a nopal on the back. What is it called?
hints: It's in the National Museum of Anthropology.
It is thought to celebrate a New Fire ceremony in the time of Moctezuma II.
Its name means “house of god” in Nahuatl and it speaks of water and fire.
questions.fun_fact: The eagle on the Teocalli doesn't hold a snake in its beak but the “atl-tlachinolli” sign, water and fire, which meant war.

media.credit: Aztec artist · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Aztec artist

questions.description: A paper so tough it survives centuries… and even your little brother with crayons.
questions.question: You’re at a crafts market looking at birds painted on amate paper. Before the Spanish Conquest, what was painted on this paper?
hints: They folded up like an accordion.
They held calendars, histories and lists of tributes.
They were the books of the peoples of Mesoamerica.
questions.fun_fact: Amate paper is made by boiling tree bark and beating the strips with a stone until they form a sheet.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: Black, sticky and not something you’d want to spread on your toast.
questions.question: Chapopote seeps out of the ground on the Gulf coast. It’s black and sticky, and today it’s used to waterproof roofs. What kind of substance is it?
hints: It forms underground over millions of years.
Veracruz and Tabasco are famous for this kind of wealth.
Pemex’s business is getting it out of the ground.
questions.fun_fact: Coastal peoples used chapopote as glue and to waterproof canoes long before refineries existed.

media.credit: Lldenke · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lldenke

questions.description: Mexico’s oldest arm workout, and no monthly gym fee.
questions.question: It’s made of volcanic stone, has three legs and is used with a long stone called a metlapil or mano. What is a metate for?
hints: You use it on your knees, pushing forward.
It’s where the dough gets made.
Afterward, the tortillas are cooked on the comal.
questions.fun_fact: Grinding on a metate was so important that many families passed theirs down from grandmother to granddaughter.

media.credit: Hiart · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hiart

questions.description: A Toltec family tree where even the dad gets his own legend.
questions.question: I led the Chichimecas before Tula's golden age, was worshipped as a god of hunting and fathered Topiltzin Quetzalcóatl. Who am I?
hints: I was shown with a bow and arrows.
The Milky Way was one of my forms.
My name means “cloud serpent.”
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica held the Quecholli month festival in his honor, with a great hunt.

media.credit: Rafael Aparicio · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rafael Aparicio

questions.description: Some flowers are for giving, and some are for eating with melted cheese.
questions.question: At a fonda, you're offered quesadillas “de flor.” The flower is orange, grows on a vine that spreads across the milpa, and is cooked with epazote. Which flower is it?
hints: The plant it grows on also gives a big, round fruit.
Its plant is one of the “three sisters” of the milpa, along with corn and beans.
Its name starts with “flor de cala…”.
questions.fun_fact: In the milpa, squash covers the ground with its big leaves, which keeps the soil moist and stops weeds from growing.

media.credit: UrendaMaria09 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: UrendaMaria09

questions.description: A chile so proud of its hometown that it took the town's name.
questions.question: Look at this chile pepper: its name comes from a Mexican city. Which one?
hints: It's a plump green chile that's often eaten pickled.
The city is famous for its coffee and its drizzly weather.
Its name can be spelled with an X or a J.
questions.fun_fact: A chipotle is a ripe jalapeño that has been dried and smoked.

media.credit: Rob Holland from Decatur, GA, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rob Holland from Decatur, GA, USA

questions.description: A giant with its arms up, as if it's been in a stick-up for 100 years.
questions.question: The saguaro grows over 12 m (40 ft) tall, sprouts arms after many years and grows only in one desert Mexico shares with the US. Which one?
hints: It's in northwestern Mexico.
It reaches the Gulf of California and Arizona.
It's named after the state whose capital is Hermosillo.
questions.fun_fact: A saguaro can take about 70 years to grow its first arm.

media.credit: Gentry George, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gentry George, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

questions.description: Before it was the drink of the gods, it was a little juice with a big future.
questions.question: I'm the sweet sap the tlachiquero scrapes from the heart of the maguey; if I'm left to ferment, I become pulque. What's my name?
hints: I'm collected fresh, before any fermenting.
My taste is a bit like something bees make.
My Spanish name joins two words: one for water and one for something sweet.
questions.fun_fact: A good pulque maguey can give several liters of aguamiel a day for months.

media.credit: Ashwin Baindur (User:AshLin) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ashwin Baindur (User:AshLin)

questions.description: A laid-back plant that spends all day hanging around the living room doing nothing.
questions.question: I'm a succulent from Mexico. I hang from pots on long stems full of plump, bluish little leaves that fall off if you touch me. What am I called?
hints: My name is a body part of an animal.
My stems hang down like something an animal swishes to chase away flies.
The animal in my name is a relative of the horse, and it brays.
questions.fun_fact: Every little leaf that falls off can grow roots and become a new plant.

media.credit: Steffen Mokosch · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steffen Mokosch

questions.description: A pumpkin that didn't want to be a lantern and chose to be delicious instead.
questions.question: Calabaza en tacha is cooked with piloncillo and cinnamon and eaten around Día de Muertos. What kind of food is it?
hints: It cooks slowly in a big pot.
The pumpkin pieces turn shiny and sticky.
It's served after the meal, with a glass of milk.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the tachas, the big pans once used on Mexico's sugar haciendas.

media.credit: John Cummings · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Cummings

questions.description: A tree that has seen more history than your school textbook.
questions.question: I'm an ahuehuete tree in Popotla. People say Hernán Cortés sat under my branches after fleeing Tenochtitlan in defeat in 1520. What am I known as?
hints: I'm in Mexico City, out near Tacuba.
Today I'm an old trunk next to a church, protected by a fence.
Since 2021 I've had a new official name: Árbol de la Noche Victoriosa.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2021 the tree's official name has been Árbol de la Noche Victoriosa (Tree of the Victorious Night), because the Mexica won that night.

media.credit: Steve Cadman from London, U.K. · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steve Cadman from London, U.K.

questions.description: The skinny, wild grandpa of the most famous corncob in the world.
questions.question: It's a wild Mexican grass with tiny ears of a few very hard kernels. About 9,000 years ago people domesticated it, and it became corn. What is it called?
hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl.
It was domesticated in the Balsas River valley.
Its name starts with “teo”, like Teotihuacan.
questions.fun_fact: An ear of teosinte has only about 10 kernels, each in a super-hard shell.

media.credit: Huntington and Page; · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: A tree so Mexican it has relatives in almost every forest in the country.
questions.question: The encino grows acorns, its wood is very hard, and Mexico has more species of it than any other country. Which group of trees is it part of?
hints: There are hundreds of species in this group around the world.
Their nuts are a favorite food of squirrels.
Their scientific name is Quercus, and their wood is used to make wine barrels.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has more than 150 species of encino, about a third of all the species in the world.

media.credit: Tomascastelazo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tomascastelazo

questions.description: A shy god jumped into the fire, and that's how the light that gives us our suntan was switched on.
questions.question: If you want to visit the place where, according to the Mexica, the gods gathered to create the Fifth Sun, which archaeological site do you go to?
hints: The Mexica gave this abandoned city its name in Nahuatl.
It was already in ruins when the Mexica arrived.
It is near Mexico City and has the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon.
questions.fun_fact: Teotihuacan means something like “the place where men become gods.”

media.credit: Chitrapa · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chitrapa

questions.description: A bone collector who never lends them to anyone… well, almost never.
questions.question: In my kingdom I keep the bones of the people of past suns. When a god came to ask for them, I gave him a conch with no holes to play. Who am I?
hints: My home is at the very bottom, on the last of nine levels.
I'm often shown as a skeleton, sometimes with owls and spiders nearby.
I'm the lord of the place of the dead, Mictlán.
questions.fun_fact: Quetzalcóatl managed to play the conch because some worms drilled holes in it and some bees made it sound.

media.credit: Didier Descouens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Didier Descouens

questions.description: Two brothers who beat the underworld in a ball game, and without any video replay.
questions.question: They are twins who beat the lords of Xibalba at the ball game and rose to the sky as the Sun and the Moon. Which Maya book tells the story of Hunahpu and his brother?
hints: It is the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya.
It also tells how the gods made humans out of corn.
Its name is often translated as “Book of the Council.”
questions.fun_fact: According to the same book, the gods tried making humans out of mud and wood before they got it right with corn.

media.credit: Simon Burchell · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Simon Burchell

questions.description: An era so windy that not even the best hairdo made it through.
questions.question: The Mexica believed the world went through several eras, or “suns.” Which god ruled the Sun of Wind?
hints: He was one of the most important creator gods.
His temples were round, so the wind could flow without anything in the way.
The Maya knew him as Kukulcan.
questions.fun_fact: According to the myth, the humans of the Sun of Wind ended up turned into monkeys.

media.credit: El Comandante · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: El Comandante

questions.description: A Mesoamerican book with a name straight out of an Italian soap opera.
questions.question: The Codex Borgia is a Mesoamerican book painted on deerskin. Why does it have an Italian family name?
questions.answer: It belonged to a Cardinal Borgia
wrong_answers: An explorer named Borgia brought it
An archaeologist named Borgia found it
hints: Today it is kept in the Vatican Library.
The Borgia family is famous in the history of the Church in Rome.
Stefano Borgia dressed in red.
questions.fun_fact: It folds like an accordion and, opened out, is about 10 meters (33 ft) long.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: A dessert that turns stale bread into a sin you're actually allowed.
questions.question: Rosca is to Día de Reyes as capirotada is to…
hints: It's a season of the year, not a single day.
During it, many people don't eat meat on Fridays.
It ends with Holy Week.
questions.fun_fact: Capirotada is made with bread, piloncillo, cheese, raisins and peanuts, and some say each ingredient has a religious meaning.

media.credit: Alejandro Lugo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alejandro Lugo

questions.description: Beans wearing a wide-brimmed hat and spurs.
questions.question: Frijoles charros are soupy, served with carne asada and typical of northern Mexico. What fried, chopped ingredient do they almost always have?
hints: It's meat.
It comes from the pig.
Lots of people eat it in strips with eggs for breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: Besides bacon, many frijoles charros recipes also add chorizo, hot dogs and ham.

media.credit: Juan Emilio Prades Bel · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Emilio Prades Bel

questions.description: A Sunday broth that makes Monday hurt a little less.
questions.question: This consomé comes with barbacoa tacos. What animal is the traditional barbacoa of Hidalgo and central Mexico made from?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It grazes in flocks on the hills of Hidalgo.
Its babies are called lambs.
questions.fun_fact: The consomé is made from the juices the meat releases while it cooks wrapped in maguey leaves inside a pit in the ground.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A dish with a miracle in its name, but no special effects.
questions.question: In Veracruz you order it at seafood stands, it's served cold and its name promises to bring you back to life. What is a «vuelve a la vida»?
hints: You eat it with a spoon.
It comes in a tall glass or a big cup.
It has shrimp, octopus, oysters and tomato sauce.
questions.fun_fact: People say the vuelve a la vida “brings you back” because it's loaded with lime, onion, cilantro and chile, all served ice cold.

media.credit: Luis Alvaz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Alvaz

questions.description: Some eggs that carry their hometown in their last name.
questions.question: The huevos motuleños in the photo are named after the town where they were invented. Which state is it in?
hints: It's a state in the southeast.
Its food is also famous for cochinita pibil.
Chichén Itzá is there.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that huevos motuleños were born in Motul in the early 20th century, in the kitchen of Jorge Siqueff.

media.credit: Skeltoac · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Skeltoac

questions.description: A meat so thin you could almost read through it.
questions.question: It's beef cut into very thin strips, salted and dried; in Oaxaca it's grilled over charcoal and goes on tlayudas. What is it called?
hints: It's sold in the smoke-filled aisle of the 20 de Noviembre market.
Before refrigerators, salting and drying meat was the way to keep it.
Its name starts with “ta.”
questions.fun_fact: At the 20 de Noviembre market in Oaxaca, you pick your raw meat and they grill it right there in an aisle full of smoke.

media.credit: Bluerasberry · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bluerasberry

questions.description: A tortilla that switched grains and moved far away from home.
questions.question: Flour tortillas are made from wheat, not corn. They're used for burritos and served with carne asada. Which part of Mexico are they typical of?
hints: It's very hot there, and there are deserts.
It's a land of big cattle ranches and cowboys.
Sonora and Chihuahua are there.
questions.fun_fact: In Sonora they make huge, paper-thin flour tortillas called “sobaqueras”.

media.credit: Vigilantcosmicpenguin · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vigilantcosmicpenguin

questions.description: A chile that got wrinkly with age but gained character.
questions.question: What dried chile, almost black with a chocolatey flavor, comes from a type of poblano and goes into mole poblano?
hints: It's one of the three classic chiles in mole poblano.
It's a cousin of the ancho chile, which is more reddish.
It's a poblano left to ripen until very dark before drying; the ancho comes from a redder one.
questions.fun_fact: Classic mole poblano uses three dried chiles: ancho, pasilla and mulato.

media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: The sweetest table of the year, and it's not even at your birthday party.
questions.question: I'm sweet and white, shaped like a little head, your name is written on my forehead, and I show up on Day of the Dead ofrendas. What am I?
hints: I'm decorated with bright colors.
I have big round eyes, but no nose.
I'm a skeleton's head, but made of candy.
questions.fun_fact: Calaveritas de azúcar are made in clay molds, using a candy-making technique called alfeñique.

media.credit: Yavidaxiu · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yavidaxiu

questions.description: Empanadas with the ocean hidden inside.
questions.question: These empanadas from the coasts of Sinaloa and Nayarit are filled with shrimp. Which group of animals do shrimp belong to?
hints: It has a hard shell.
It has lots of legs and antennae.
Crabs and lobsters belong to the same group.
questions.fun_fact: Shrimp turn pink when cooked because the heat releases a pigment called astaxanthin.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A drink so old it has its own fair and even its own goddess.
questions.question: You're at the Feria del Pulque, and a mural shows the Mexica goddess of the maguey. Who is she?
hints: In the myth, the first maguey plant grew from her.
She was the mother of the Centzon Totochtin, the 400 rabbits of pulque.
Her name starts with “Maya…”.
questions.fun_fact: Before it ferments, the sweet sap taken from the maguey is called aguamiel (honey water).

media.credit: ArCaRa · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ArCaRa

questions.description: An appointment so important that people walk to it… for several days.
questions.question: Her small statue is made of corn-stalk paste, and thousands of pilgrims walk over 100 km (62 miles) through Jalisco's mountains from Ameca to see her. Which Virgin is she?
wrong_answers: The Virgin of San Juan de los Lagos
hints: Her shrine is in the western mountains of Jalisco, far from Guadalajara.
The town of her shrine carries the surname of the independence hero Ignacio Allende.
Her name starts with “T.”
questions.fun_fact: Talpa de Allende is a Pueblo Mágico, famous for its colorful little figures made of chicle that pilgrims take home as souvenirs.

media.credit: Christian Frausto Bernal · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Christian Frausto Bernal

questions.description: A parade so cheerful that even the puppets grow 3 meters tall to see it.
questions.question: In Oaxaca, before a saint's feast, a parade fills the streets with a band, giant cane “monos” and cloth globes called marmotas. What is it called?
hints: It usually goes out at night, among fireworks and lights.
Young women dance with decorated baskets on their heads.
Its name comes from the Latin “calendae”, the first day of the month.
questions.fun_fact: The marmota of a calenda is a big cloth ball on a pole that someone spins while dancing.

media.credit: User: (WT-shared) Anyludes at  wts wikivoyage · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User: (WT-shared) Anyludes at  wts wikivoyage

questions.description: A fair where even the cider comes straight from the tree.
questions.question: In which month is the Feria de la Manzana (Apple Fair) of Zacatlán, Puebla, held?
hints: It falls on the feast of the town's patron saint, the Virgen de la Asunción.
It's rainy season and harvest time in the mountains.
It's the month right before Mexico's Independence Day celebrations.
questions.fun_fact: Zacatlán is also famous for its big flower clock and its factories that build giant clocks.

media.credit: Marc-Lautenbacher · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Marc-Lautenbacher

questions.description: A fair named after a saint people pray to for the impossible, like finding a parking spot.
questions.question: Every May, the Feria de Santa Rita honors Saint Rita of Cascia, patron saint of a state capital in northern Mexico. Which one?
hints: It's in the north, surrounded by desert and mountains.
Miguel Hidalgo was executed by firing squad there in 1811.
It's the capital of the country's largest state.
questions.fun_fact: The feast of Saint Rita of Cascia is on May 22, which is why the fair falls in that month.

media.credit: blmcalifornia · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: blmcalifornia

questions.description: A little smudge on the forehead that nobody rushes to wash off.
questions.question: Look at the photo: on which day of the year do people leave church with this cross on their forehead?
hints: It comes right after the last day of carnival.
It marks the start of Lent.
It always falls in the middle of the week.
questions.fun_fact: Because it depends on the date of Easter, Ash Wednesday can fall anywhere between February 4 and March 10.

media.credit: Oxh973 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Oxh973

questions.description: In Veracruz, people don't ask what time it is; they ask whether it has come in yet.
questions.question: In Veracruz they say “entró un norte”: it comes between October and March, closes the port and makes temperatures drop. What is a norte?
hints: It doesn't come from the warm sea; it comes from cold lands.
It arrives with the cold fronts of winter.
It messes up everyone's hair on the malecón and blows their hats away.
questions.fun_fact: When a norte blows very hard, the authorities sometimes close the port of Veracruz to ships.

media.credit: SMU Central University Libraries · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SMU Central University Libraries

questions.description: Your grandma thinks it's scarier than any horror movie.
questions.question: It's the cool damp of the night: laundry left out is wet by morning, and grandmas say never go out in it without a jacket. What is it called in Mexico?
hints: It only shows up after the sun has gone down.
It isn't rain: it falls without you seeing it.
Its name sounds like the English word for very calm.
questions.fun_fact: Long ago, “el sereno” was also the night watchman who walked the streets calling out the time.

media.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dennis G. Jarvis

questions.description: Mexican weather: you leave home with one plan and come back with another.
questions.question: “I flip umbrellas inside out, make tin roofs rattle and steal kites without asking; I'm much more than a breeze.” What am I?
hints: I don't get anyone wet.
You can't see me, but you can hear me whistle.
My name is something that blows, made giant-sized.
questions.fun_fact: In La Ventosa, on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, the wind blows so steadily that hundreds of wind turbines stand there.

media.credit: Conor from Jhongli · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Conor from Jhongli

questions.description: She had goggles, boots, and more fans than plenty of TV stars.
questions.question: Frida was a Mexican Navy Labrador who wore goggles and little boots and became famous in the 2017 earthquake. What was her job?
wrong_answers: Guarding the boats at the port
hints: Her little boots protected her from broken glass and bits of metal.
She used her nose after earthquakes.
She worked alongside rescue teams.
questions.fun_fact: Frida retired in 2019 with an honors ceremony held by the Navy.

media.credit: Kylelovesyou · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kylelovesyou

questions.description: Three rules your teacher repeats more often than the 2 times table.
questions.question: The drill alarm goes off at school and the teacher says: “No corro, no grito, no empujo” (“I don't run, I don't shout, I don't push”). What is that phrase for?
hints: It's used when you have to leave the classroom.
If everyone runs and pushes, someone could fall.
It's for practicing what to do in an earthquake.
questions.fun_fact: Some schools add a fourth rule, “no regreso” (“I don't go back”), so nobody goes back for their backpack.

media.credit: U.S. Army photo by Elena Baladelli · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: U.S. Army photo by Elena Baladelli

questions.description: A genre with more verses than the audience has patience for.
questions.question: It's a song that tells a story. It told of the deeds of Villa and Zapata, and “La Adelita” is a famous example. What is this genre called?
hints: It was sung from town to town to tell what was happening.
Today there are also norteño versions of this genre.
Its name comes from the Spanish verb for “to run.”
questions.fun_fact: During the Revolution, corridos worked like newscasts, bringing news of the battles to people who couldn't read.

media.credit: SMU Central University Libraries · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SMU Central University Libraries

questions.description: A list of six demands that shook the government more than any final exam.
questions.question: In 1968, students in Mexico handed in a six-point list of demands. Which police force did they want abolished?
hints: It was the capital's riot police.
They had stormed schools by force in July 1968.
Its name comes from the soldiers who once threw grenades.
questions.fun_fact: The list also demanded the repeal of the crime of “social dissolution,” which was used to jail opponents.

media.credit: Cacum2 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cacum2

questions.description: A song with wings that every mariachi knows by heart.
questions.question: In Mexico, when “Las golondrinas” is sung at a party or a ceremony, what does it mean?
hints: It's almost always sung at the end, not at the start.
It's about a bird that flies far from its nest.
You hear it when someone leaves, retires or finishes school.
questions.fun_fact: “Las golondrinas” was written by Narciso Serradell in the 19th century, and Mexicans have sung it to say goodbye for more than 100 years.

media.credit: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles J. Sharp

questions.description: A furry neighbor who shows up at night when nobody invited him.
questions.question: The word “mapache” (raccoon) comes from Nahuatl. Roughly, what does it mean?
questions.answer: The one who grabs everything with its hands
wrong_answers: The one with the striped tail
The one who only comes out at night
The one who wears a black mask
hints: The name is about something the raccoon does, not about its color.
It seems to “wash” its food in water.
Its front paws look like little hands.
questions.fun_fact: A raccoon's front paws are so sensitive that it can recognize its food by touch, without looking at it.

media.credit: Rhododendrites · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rhododendrites

questions.description: This snake comes with its own built-in maraca.
questions.question: Look at the photo: this snake shakes the tip of its tail to make a rattling sound. Which country has more species of it than any other?
hints: It's a country in the Americas.
Many of them live in its northern and central deserts and mountains.
Some say the snake on its coat of arms is one of them.
questions.fun_fact: Every time a rattlesnake sheds its skin, a new segment is added to its rattle.

media.credit: Holger Krisp · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Holger Krisp

questions.description: A colorful beak that won't move in just anywhere.
questions.question: In which of these Mexican states do toucans NOT live in the wild?
hints: The toucan needs tropical rainforest and lots of fruit.
It likes places that are hot, humid and full of tall trees.
This northern state is famous for its desert and the Barranca del Cobre (Copper Canyon).
questions.fun_fact: In southeastern Mexico the toucan is also called “pico de canoa” (canoe beak) because of the shape of its bill.

media.credit: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles J. Sharp

questions.description: A green vegetable shaped like a pear that nobody ever mistakes for a pear.
questions.question: Look at this vegetable. Its name comes from the language of a Mesoamerican people. Which one?
hints: They were the most powerful people in Mesoamerica when the Spanish arrived.
Their legend says they founded their city where they saw an eagle on a nopal cactus.
We also know them as the Aztecs.
questions.fun_fact: Words like “chocolate,” “tomato” and “avocado” also come from Nahuatl.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: A tree with a tongue-twister name and a reputation as a grandma's remedy.
questions.question: At a market herb stall, you buy cuachalalate for a traditional stomach tea. What part of the tree are you being sold?
hints: It's sold in hard, dry pieces.
It's an outer part taken off the tree.
It's what covers the trunk.
questions.fun_fact: Cuachalalate grows in the dry forests of western and southern Mexico.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: In Mexico almost everything comes from the milpa, but someone snuck into this party.
questions.question: Which of these foods is NOT made with corn?
hints: Three of them come from the ear of corn.
The one you're looking for is bought at the bakery.
It's made with wheat flour.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has dozens of native corn varieties, in colors like blue, red, purple and white.

media.author: Tomascastelazo

questions.description: Without it, the mariachi would sound like it forgot something at home.
questions.question: In a mariachi band, which instrument plays the bass?
hints: The back of its body bulges out in a V shape.
The musician almost hugs it to play it.
It's related to the guitar, but much bigger.
questions.fun_fact: The guitarrón is often played by plucking two strings at once, in octaves, so its bass sounds louder without an amplifier.

media.author: Carlos Felipe Pardo from Washington, United States

questions.description: A dessert that could cost you nothing… or cost you twice.
questions.question: By tradition, you can challenge the merenguero: win and the meringue is free, lose and you pay double. Which game decides it?
hints: All you need is something you carry in your pocket.
You have to pick one of two sides.
You flip a coin: águila o sol.
questions.fun_fact: Meringues are made by beating egg whites with sugar until they turn light and fluffy.

media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: Water in such a hurry to get down that it doesn't even say goodbye to the mountain.
questions.question: Look at the photo: these Chiapas waterfalls share their name with the draft of air that, grandmas say, gives you a stiff neck. What are they called?
hints: They're near Comitán, on the San Vicente River.
Their tallest drop is called the Velo de Novia (Bridal Veil).
The name sounds like a chiflido, a whistle.
questions.fun_fact: The Velo de Novia at El Chiflón falls from about 120 m (394 ft) high.

media.author: User:Angel06x

questions.description: A forest that takes up more room on the map than a cousin asleep on the couch.
questions.question: It covers slopes along Mexico's Pacific side, from Sonora to Chiapas, and is the tropical vegetation that covers the most land in Mexico. What is it called?
hints: Its trees rarely grow taller than 15 m (49 ft).
In the dry season it looks gray and colorless.
Its name says it loses its leaves.
questions.fun_fact: The palo mulato (gumbo-limbo) is nicknamed the “tourist tree” because its red bark peels like sunburned skin.

media.author: Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center

questions.description: They arrive with a number, like at the tortillería, but instead of tortillas they hand out cold.

hints: The season runs from September to May, about eight months.
If 20 have come by winter, there are still more on the way.
Roughly one arrives each week.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's cold front count starts again at number 1 every September.

questions.question: The Sierra de Manantlán biosphere reserve, between Jalisco and Colima, was created after a wild relative of a crop was found there. Which crop?
hints: The find was made by a University of Guadalajara student in the late 1970s.
This crop was domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago.
The wild plant is a teosinte that lives for several years.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to this perennial teosinte, scientists dream of a corn that doesn't have to be planted again every year.

media.author: Juan Pablo Esparza

questions.description: A young woman who didn't need a uniform to chase an army out of town.
questions.question: In Parral, Chihuahua, a statue honors Elisa Griensen, who in 1916 led the town against US soldiers. Which general led their expedition?
hints: The soldiers were hunting for Pancho Villa.
He later commanded his country's troops in Europe during World War I.
His nickname was “Black Jack.”
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that Elisa scolded the town's men for not defending it, then went out with women and children to throw stones.

media.author: Pedro Eduardo Romero Vázquez

questions.description: A school trip so exciting that even the bus shows up eager to learn.
questions.question: Your school takes a trip to Universum, at the UNAM's Ciudad Universitaria. What kind of museum is it?
hints: Its name sounds like something very, very big.
There you learn through experiments and games.
It has halls about the human body, energy and space.
questions.fun_fact: Universum opened in 1992 at Ciudad Universitaria, a campus that UNESCO named a World Heritage Site in 2007.

media.author: Daniel Case

questions.description: Mexico doesn't like to brag, but on this one it's off the charts.
questions.question: Mexico belongs to the group of megadiverse countries. What do these countries have plenty of?
hints: It has to do with living nature.
Think of what you find in the Lacandon Jungle, the reefs of Cozumel and the Sonoran Desert.
Another word for it is “biodiversity”.
questions.fun_fact: Only about 17 countries in the world are megadiverse, and together they hold about 70% of the planet's species.

media.author: Jorge Mendoza

questions.description: Land of strawberries, cajeta and car factories… but someone sneaked into the photo.
questions.question: Which of these states is NOT part of the Bajío region?
hints: The Bajío is a region of valleys and plains in central Mexico.
It is famous for its farm fields and its car factories.
The odd one out has a long coast on the Gulf of Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: Although its name means “lowland,” the region sits about 1,800 meters (5,900 feet) above sea level.

media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A candy whose name sounds like a kitchen accident, but it's made on purpose.

hints: Cajeta from Celaya, in Guanajuato, is famous all over Mexico

Its babies are called kids
questions.fun_fact: Cajeta gets its name from the little wooden boxes (cajitas) it used to be sold in.

media.author: Cristina Zapata Pérez

hints: Lots of bread fits on it
It's usually made of aluminum
In restaurants, waiters carry plates on one
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to the tongs, everyone picks their own bread without touching it with their hands.

media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A dessert that can't sit still, not even inside the oven.
questions.question: I'm a two-layer dessert, and in the oven my layers swap places all by themselves. What am I?
hints: I get drizzled with cajeta or caramel
People call me the “impossible cake”
My name joins my two layers
questions.fun_fact: The cake batter is lighter than the flan, so it rises while the flan sinks to the bottom.

media.author: Kirt Edblom from Albany, Oregon, United States

questions.description: The flan's cousin who got all dressed up to go out.
questions.question: Which ingredient makes flan napolitano denser than classic flan?
hints: It's white and spreadable
It's made from milk and sold in the supermarket fridge
It comes in a little bar wrapped in silver foil
questions.fun_fact: Flan came to Mexico with the Spanish, and Mexicans made it their own with cajeta, cheese and even rompope.

questions.description: The fair has it all: cotton candy, shouting, and this mystery word.
questions.question: At the fair, they're announcing a títere show. What is a títere?

It has a face, a head and clothes, but it can't move by itself.
A hidden person lends it their hands and voice.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico's National Puppet Museum is in Huamantla, Tlaxcala.

questions.description: A stone that went to the trouble of painting itself on the inside.
questions.question: It's a stone with colored bands, it forms inside volcanic rock, and the finest marbles were once made from it. What stone is it?
hints: Its name comes from a river on the island of Sicily.

In English, fine old-fashioned marbles were called “aggies” after it.
questions.fun_fact: Agate gets its bands because the mineral builds up layer by layer inside hollows in the rock.

questions.description: A word that in Spain names a wine grape, and in Mexico means something very different.
questions.question: In Mexico, what are “garnachas”?

Sopes, chalupas and fried quesadillas fall into this group.
They leave your napkins covered in oil stains.
questions.fun_fact: In Veracruz, garnachas are also a snack of their own: small fried tortillas with shredded meat, salsa and potato.

media.author: Daniel Case

questions.description: A Christmas party where even the front door gets its own lines.
questions.question: At the posadas, one group sings outside as pilgrims. Who do the people answering from inside the house play?

In Spanish they're called “mesoneros,” from “mesón,” an old-time inn.
questions.fun_fact: At first the people inside reply “Aquí no es mesón, sigan adelante” (“This is no inn, go on ahead”), and only at the end, when they recognize Joseph and Mary, do they sing “Entren, santos peregrinos” (“Come in, holy pilgrims”).

questions.description: A date that isn't a holiday, but fires the starting gun for the season of ponche and piñatas.
questions.question: In Mexico, the posadas start on December 16 exactly. Why that day?
questions.answer: To have nine nights, like the months of pregnancy
wrong_answers: To have twelve nights, like the apostles
To have seven nights, like the days of Creation
To have forty nights, like Lent
hints: Each night, people go door to door singing to ask for shelter.
The posadas end right on Christmas Eve.
It's how long it takes for a baby to be born.
questions.fun_fact: The posadas come from the “misas de aguinaldo,” special Christmas masses the friars held in New Spain, as at the Acolman convent in the late 16th century.

media.author: Donald Olszewski

questions.description: A Christmas play with more plot twists than a telenovela and more jokes than a comedy show.
questions.question: In Mexican pastorelas, which character tries to trick the shepherds so they never reach Bethlehem?
