He usually comes on stage dressed in red, with horns and a tail.
questions.fun_fact: Pastorelas came with the friars in colonial times to teach the Christmas story, and today many of them are comedies full of jokes.

media.author: Nesnad

questions.description: Outside, nothing but colored paper; inside, a secret almost nobody has seen.
questions.question: Traditionally, what was inside spiked piñatas like this one to hold the candy?

It's a container also used in the kitchen for ponche or beans.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the seven spikes of the piñata stand for the seven deadly sins, and breaking it means beating evil.

media.credit: jleonelss · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: jleonelss

questions.description: Sunsets, a malecón, and an ice cream melting faster than your sunscreen.
questions.question: This beach city, with its crowned church by the sea, is world famous. Which city is it?

Its name starts with “Puerto.”
questions.fun_fact: The film “The Night of the Iguana,” shot in 1963 on Mismaloya beach, made this fishing village famous around the world.

media.author: David Stanley from Nanaimo, Canada

questions.description: A sweet so firm you slice it like cheese.
questions.question: You're at the Portal de Dulces in Morelia and you buy an ate. What is it made of?

It's cooked slowly in big pots until it gets very thick.
It's made from the pulp of something that grows on trees.
questions.fun_fact: Quince ate is eaten with cheese, and in Michoacán guava ate is one of the most popular kinds.

media.author: Adavyd

questions.description: A miner with a stone slab on his back and more guts than a luchador at his first match.
questions.question: The Pípila Monument honors the miner who set fire to the door of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas. Whose army went in next?

The Grito de Dolores had rung out that same month.
It was led by a priest.
questions.fun_fact: From the monument you can see all of Guanajuato, and you can ride a funicular up to it.

media.author: August Dominus

questions.description: A dive here isn't scored with a 10, but with applause and a big shout.
questions.question: You're watching the La Quebrada cliff divers leap into the sea. Which city are you in?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
It's the most famous beach town in Guerrero.
Its name starts with “A”.
questions.fun_fact: The La Quebrada divers jump from about 35 m (115 ft) up, and they have been doing it since the 1930s.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A sea so full of life that the fish need traffic lights.
questions.question: Which of these animals does NOT live in the sea off Loreto, in the Gulf of California?
hints: Loreto is in Baja California Sur, on the Sea of Cortez.
This animal lives in the Caribbean and in rivers of southeastern Mexico.
People call it the “sea cow.”
questions.fun_fact: Loreto was founded in 1697 and was the first capital of the Californias.

media.credit: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada

questions.description: The only bread that turns red before you even bite it.
questions.question: A pambazo is a soft bread roll filled with potato and chorizo and browned on the comal. What gives it its red color?
hints: The bread gets dipped before it's browned.
It comes from a dried chile.
It's the same chile used in many red pozoles.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from “pan bazo”, a simple bread made with coarse, unrefined flour.

media.credit: Cristina Zapata Pérez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cristina Zapata Pérez

questions.description: Friars who spent weeks on a ship praying, mostly not to get seasick.
questions.question: They arrived in New Spain in 1526 and wore a white habit with a black cape. Which religious order were they?
hints: They were the second order to arrive, after the friars in brown habits.
Friar Bartolomé de las Casas was one of them.
Their founder was a Spanish saint named Domingo de Guzmán.
questions.fun_fact: The old Santo Domingo monastery in Oaxaca now holds a museum and a huge garden of native plants.

media.credit: Amigooswal1 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Amigooswal1

questions.description: A name that sounds like a wild animal, but ends up in party clothes.
questions.question: On the coast of Oaxaca, some weavers use coyuchi in their huipiles. What is coyuchi?
hints: It comes from a plant, not from an animal or an insect.
Its color doesn't come from any dye.
It's a relative of the white fluff used to make manta cloth.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Nahuatl and is linked to the coyote, because its color looks like the animal's fur.

media.credit: David.Clay.Photography · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David.Clay.Photography

questions.description: A machine you weave with using your feet while your hands do something else.
questions.question: You're in Teotitlán del Valle watching a weaver make a rug on a treadle loom. Where did this kind of loom come to Mexico from?
hints: Before it arrived, people in Mesoamerica wove on the backstrap loom.
It arrived in the 16th century.
The conquistadors brought it.
questions.fun_fact: In Teotitlán, the wool rugs are colored with natural dyes such as cochineal and indigo.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: A mountain village with a craft you won't learn at the stationery store.
questions.question: The Otomí village of San Pablito, in Pahuatlán, Puebla, is famous for making a handmade paper. Which one?
hints: It has been made without machines since pre-Hispanic times.
It's made from tree bark.
In Guerrero, people paint pictures of birds and flowers on it.
questions.fun_fact: To make amate paper, the bark fibers are boiled and then pounded flat with a stone.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A villain with a black cape and far too much free time for making bets.
questions.question: In “The Book of Life,” the villain is named Xibalba, a name that comes from the Maya. What was Xibalba to them?
hints: It appears in the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K’iche’ Maya.
The twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque went down there to play the ball game against its lords.
It was the place of the dead, beneath the earth.
questions.fun_fact: “The Book of Life” was directed by Mexican filmmaker Jorge R. Gutiérrez and produced by Guillermo del Toro.

media.credit: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium

questions.description: The guest nobody invites, yet she always shows up right on time.
questions.question: I appear in calaveritas literarias and no one escapes me, rich or poor. In Mexico they call me la Pelona. Who am I?
hints: Everyone will meet me someday.
They also call me la Flaca and la Huesuda.
La Catrina is my most elegant version.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, death has dozens of nicknames, such as la Calaca, la Tilica, la Huesuda and la Dientona.

media.credit: Thirty two · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thirty two

questions.description: A day on the calendar with a very exclusive guest list.
questions.question: For Día de Muertos, many families in Mexico dedicate November 1 to one special group of the departed. Which one?
hints: This group of souls is believed to be the first to arrive.
Their ofrenda gets toys, candy and milk.
On this day, families often set out the departed's small clothes and favorite little treats.
questions.fun_fact: In many parts of Mexico, departed children are given tiny plates and cups, sized for their little hands.

media.credit: Karla Andrew · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Karla Andrew

questions.description: A drink named after a fierce animal that turns out to be as sweet as dessert.
questions.question: The torito, a party drink from Veracruz, is made with aguardiente and fruit or peanuts. What other ingredient makes it creamy?
hints: It's not what goes into rompope.
It comes in a can and is very sweet.
It's a dairy product used a lot in desserts like flan.
questions.fun_fact: The most famous toritos are peanut, soursop or mango, and they're sold in Tlacotalpan and Alvarado.

media.credit: Comisión Mexicana de Filmaciones from México D. F., México · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Comisión Mexicana de Filmaciones from México D. F., México

questions.description: Red, a little spicy, and more famous in Jalisco than many mariachi singers.
questions.question: Jalisco's sangrita is red and spicy, made with orange, chile, and pomegranate or tomato. What is it served for?
wrong_answers: To pour over tacos al pastor
hints: It's served in a small glass.
You sip it slowly, taking turns with another drink.
Its partner comes in a caballito.
questions.fun_fact: The original sangrita from Chapala had no tomato: its red color came from pomegranate and chile.

media.credit: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico

questions.description: A soda that travels north and comes back a celebrity.
questions.question: In the United States, many people hunt for “Mexican Coke” in glass bottles because they say it tastes different. What is it sweetened with?
hints: It's a very old sweetener, much older than soda.
It comes from a tall plant grown in Veracruz.
It's the same sugar your grandma always used.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States, the regular version is sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup, which is why the Mexican one became famous.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: A hero so big there's room for a whole staircase inside him.
questions.question: On the island of Janitzio, you can climb up inside the statue of Morelos all the way to his raised fist. About how tall is it?
hints: You can see it from far away across Lake Pátzcuaro, but it's no skyscraper.
It's much taller than a house, but much shorter than the Torre Latinoamericana.
It's between 30 and 50 meters (100 and 165 ft).
questions.fun_fact: Inside, the staircase is lined with murals that tell the story of Morelos's life.

media.credit: Isaacvp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isaacvp

questions.description: Don Porfirio didn't have Waze, but he really, really wanted to lay down tracks.
questions.question: When Porfirio Díaz took power in 1876, Mexico had about 640 km (400 mi) of railway. How much did it have by around 1910?
hints: The growth was huge, but Mexico isn't big enough to circle the world in rails.
Over those 34 years, an average of several hundred kilometers were built each year.
The figure is close to half of the way around the Earth.
questions.fun_fact: The railway from Mexico City to Veracruz opened in 1873, before Díaz came to power.

media.credit: William Henry Jackson · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: William Henry Jackson

questions.description: From general to supplier of inventions: the strangest career of the 19th century.
questions.question: Exiled in New York, Santa Anna gave Thomas Adams resin from a Mexican tree to make rubber. It didn't work. What did Adams invent with it?
hints: Adams turned his failed experiment into something cheap sold in every corner store.
The resin came from the chicozapote (sapodilla), a tree of the Maya forest.
In Mexico it's called chicle.
questions.fun_fact: Adams started selling his gum in the United States in the 1870s, and his last name became a famous brand.

media.credit: Adityamadhav83 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adityamadhav83

questions.description: Don Porfirio said something meant for American readers, and Mexico never forgot it.
questions.question: In 1908, Porfirio Díaz told a US magazine that Mexico was ready for democracy. Which journalist interviewed him?
hints: He was Canadian and wrote for US newspapers.
His last name was joined to Díaz's in the name of the famous interview.
His first name was James.
questions.fun_fact: Those statements encouraged Francisco I. Madero to write his book “La sucesión presidencial en 1910” (The Presidential Succession in 1910).

media.credit: Bain News Service · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bain News Service

questions.description: Long before loudspeakers, the Mexica already had their own megaphone.
questions.question: In Aztec dance it is blown through the tip like a trumpet, and the Mexica played it to call people to ceremonies. What is this instrument made of?
hints: The Mexica had no cows or bulls.
It comes from an animal that lived in water.
It was brought from the coast, and it once had a resident who carried its house on its back.
questions.fun_fact: When the caracol (conch) is blown, players often greet the four directions: north, south, east and west.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: Running shoes with zero cushioning and zero sports stores involved.
questions.question: Rarámuri runner Lorena Ramírez won ultramarathons in traditional huaraches. What are their soles made of?
hints: The Rarámuri make these huaraches themselves, from cheap materials they have at hand.
It is a recycled material that once had another use.
It comes from a car or a truck.
questions.fun_fact: In 2017, Lorena Ramírez won the Cerro Rojo ultramarathon, 50 km (31 miles) in Puebla, running in a skirt and huaraches.

media.credit: Robert FERREOL · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert FERREOL

questions.description: A chile that got so fancy it only goes out with crema and elote.
questions.question: Making rajas de poblano takes several kitchen steps. Which of these is NOT one of them?
hints: Think about the dish's name.
Rajas come to the plate in a shape you can see at a glance.
If you do this step, you don't get strips anymore, you get a sauce.
questions.fun_fact: Roasted poblanos go into a bag or under a cloth for a few minutes so they “sweat” and the skin peels off easily.

media.credit: Jonathan Cutrer from San Angelo, Texas, United States · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jonathan Cutrer from San Angelo, Texas, United States

questions.description: The snack that always shows up when someone says “Want to come over and watch the game?”
questions.question: Take a close look: what snack is this?
hints: They're made from something found on almost every table in Mexico.
They're cut into triangles before frying.
They're served with beans or salsa, or in chilaquiles.
questions.fun_fact: Chilaquiles are made with totopos covered in green or red salsa.

media.credit: BrokenSphere · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: BrokenSphere

questions.description: A salsa with an innocent face that can make you cry.
questions.question: If you eat this salsa and your mouth is on fire, which ingredient is to blame?
hints: It's the bravest ingredient in the salsa.
There are many kinds: habanero, serrano, jalapeño…
In Mexico, burning your mouth this way is called “enchilarse”, and the word hides its name.
questions.fun_fact: The heat in a chile comes from capsaicin, and most of it sits in the white veins inside.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: Mashed beans that land on the plate ready to go with a good plate of chilaquiles.

hints: Before they reach the pan, the beans are already cooked in a pot.

The Spanish name “frijoles refritos” means “well-fried beans.”
questions.fun_fact: The English name “refried beans” came from translating the Spanish “re” too literally, as if they were fried twice.

media.credit: Ruth Hartnup · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ruth Hartnup

questions.description: Beans that people in the southeast wouldn't trade for anything, not even at breakfast.
questions.question: They're small, shiny beans, their broth turns almost purple, and in southern Mexico they're cooked with epazote. Which beans are they?
hints: They're often served refried next to breakfast eggs.
They're the favorite in Veracruz, Oaxaca and Yucatán.
They're the color of the night.
questions.fun_fact: Epazote goes into beans for its flavor, and many people say it also makes them easier to digest.

media.credit: Vegan Feast Catering · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vegan Feast Catering

questions.description: A market with so many aisles that even the GPS asks for help getting out.
questions.question: It sits next to La Merced in Mexico City. What is mostly sold at the Mercado de Sonora?
hints: It's right downtown, and its aisles are always packed.
There they can give you a “limpia” with branches and an egg.
People call it “the witches' market.”
questions.fun_fact: Besides its mystical aisles, it is famous for its toys, piñatas and pottery.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A painter who got tired of painting walls and decided to build some very, very dark ones of his own.
questions.question: Diego Rivera designed it, it's made of volcanic stone and it looks like a pyramid. What did he create the Anahuacalli for?
wrong_answers: To live there with Frida Kahlo
To use it as an observatory
To open a school of painting
hints: Rivera was a passionate collector.
He gathered thousands of pieces made long before the Spanish arrived.
It displays clay and stone figures from ancient cultures of Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: Rivera gathered more than 50,000 pre-Hispanic pieces for his collection.

media.credit: Randal Sheppard · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Randal Sheppard

questions.description: A building so shiny that on a sunny day you should visit it wearing sunglasses.
questions.question: Carlos Slim founded it in Polanco, thousands of hexagonal aluminum tiles cover it, and it holds many Rodin sculptures. Which museum is it?
hints: Admission is free.
Its shape looks like a twisted hourglass.
It's named after its founder's wife.
questions.fun_fact: Its building is covered with about 16,000 hexagonal aluminum tiles.

media.credit: Erik Drost from United States · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Erik Drost from United States

questions.description: A volcano that's more famous as a model than as a mountain.
questions.question: This snowy volcano next to Popocatépetl is famous for the shape of its outline. What does it look like?
wrong_answers: An old man with a cane
hints: Its name in Nahuatl describes exactly that shape.

According to legend, it's a princess waiting for her warrior.
questions.fun_fact: The parts of Iztaccíhuatl are named after body parts: climbers head for “the chest”, its highest summit.

media.credit: Carlos Adampol Galindo from DF, México · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Adampol Galindo from DF, México

questions.description: A lake in Veracruz that is more famous than a lot of TV stars.
questions.question: This is Lake Catemaco, in Veracruz. What kind of people is it famous for all over Mexico?

They do “limpias” (cleansings) with herbs and eggs.
questions.fun_fact: On an island in Lake Catemaco lives a colony of monkeys that were brought there for a scientific study.

media.credit: panza.rayada · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: panza.rayada

questions.description: A necklace of natural swimming pools that a space rock left behind as a souvenir.

The ring is too big to see from the ground.
Driving across it by road would take about two hours.
questions.fun_fact: The crater was found in the 1970s thanks to measurements taken while searching for oil; the ring of cenotes was linked to it later.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT

questions.description: Not river, not sea: water that just can't make up its mind.
questions.question: In the Celestún estuary in Yucatán, fresh water from springs mixes with seawater. What is this kind of water called?
hints: It's not good to drink.
It has some salt, but less than the sea.
The word also describes a slightly salty, unpleasant taste.
questions.fun_fact: The flamingos of Celestún are pink because of the tiny crustaceans they eat.

media.credit: Gildardo Sánchez · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gildardo Sánchez

questions.description: A god so old the candles wouldn't fit on his birthday cake… so he lit a bonfire instead.
questions.question: Xiuhtecuhtli, the lord of fire, presided over the New Fire ceremony. How often did the Mexica hold it?
hints: It was when their two calendars lined up again: the 365-day one and the 260-day one.

media.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

questions.description: A game so old the referee probably wore feathers.

wrong_answers: To tell the time by their shadow
hints: They were set high up on the walls of the court.
Players hit the rubber ball with their hips, not their hands.
Doing it was so hard that a player who managed it usually won the game on the spot.

media.credit: Katja Schulz from Washington, D. C., USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Katja Schulz from Washington, D. C., USA

questions.description: Long skirts, ruffles and flowers in the hair: on the Isthmus, getting dressed is a full production.
questions.question: The traje de tehuana, like the ones worn in Juchitán, Oaxaca, became world-famous thanks to a painter who wore it every day. Who?
hints: She was Mexican and lived in Coyoacán.
She painted herself in this dress in several self-portraits.
She was married to Diego Rivera.
questions.fun_fact: In Juchitán, women are famous for running the markets and the fiestas called velas.

media.credit: MaloMalverde · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Flickr via Openverse
media.author: MaloMalverde

questions.description: The Purépecha gave their main god a real tongue-twister of a name; now it's your turn to translate it.
questions.question: Curicaueri was the main god of the Purépecha, patron of their kings and worshipped in Tzintzuntzan. What does his name mean?

The Purépecha saw him as a god of the sky and of war.
His followers offered him firewood.
questions.fun_fact: The yácatas of Tzintzuntzan, next to Lake Pátzcuaro, were temples with a very unusual shape that mixes rectangles and semicircles.

media.credit: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium

questions.description: The ancients kept their calendars up to date, and without a single phone app.

media.credit: HJPD · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: When the capital empties out, someone has to take charge of the move.

It was the political capital of the Zapotecs, not their great religious center.
Its name starts with Z, like “Zapotec.”
questions.fun_fact: Tombs 1 and 2 at Zaachila were excavated in 1962 and held rich offerings of gold, turquoise and pottery.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A host so polite he changes the decor depending on who knocks at the door.
questions.question: In “El compadre Mendoza” (1934), a hacienda owner swaps the portrait in his living room to suit each visitor and ends up betraying his compadre, General Felipe Nieto. Which side was Nieto on?

Mendoza hung Huerta's or Carranza's portrait depending on who arrived; for Nieto he put up a third one.
Nieto's side fought under the cry “Land and liberty!”
questions.fun_fact: “El compadre Mendoza” is considered one of the best Mexican films of all time.

media.credit: J.Godinez · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: J.Godinez

questions.description: If you see him on horseback looking grumpy, don’t even think about borrowing his sombrero.

His real name was Doroteo Arango.
questions.fun_fact: Pancho Villa signed a contract with a US film company so it could film his battles.

media.credit: ismael villafranco · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ismael villafranco

questions.description: An artist who never minded drawing all over the walls.
questions.question: I was born in Guanajuato, I painted Mexico’s history on the walls of the Palacio Nacional, and I married the same painter twice. Who am I?
hints: I am one of the great Mexican muralists.

media.credit: Oescalona · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: She marched on foot behind the troops with a cooking pot in one hand and plenty of courage in the other.

questions.description: Some families just can't wait for the party to start.

It happened on November 18.

media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: A nickname earned in battle that he could never shake off.

questions.description: A building that changed plans more times than a family on vacation.

questions.description: In 1915, the presidential chair came with a revolving door.

This object rings in church towers to call people to Mass.
questions.fun_fact: The song says the Virgin's comb is made of “plata fina” (fine silver) and her hair is made of gold.

media.credit: KKPCW · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: KKPCW

questions.description: A rhythm that came from very far away and moved in for good with an accordion and a cowboy hat.
questions.question: The polka, still alive in norteño music, reached northern Mexico in the 19th century. Who brought it?
hints: They settled in northern Mexico and in Texas.
They also brought the accordion, which every norteño band has today.
They came from the land of Oktoberfest and from Bohemia.
questions.fun_fact: The polka was born around 1830 in Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic.

media.credit: Joe Mabel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Mabel

questions.description: It can't walk anymore, but it can still make you scream in the kitchen.
questions.question: In the famous Mexican song “La cucaracha,” what kind of animal is the cucaracha?
hints: Lots of people scream when they find one in the kitchen.
It has antennae and six little legs.
It's a distant relative of the cricket, just like Cri-Cri.
questions.fun_fact: “La cucaracha” became famous during the Mexican Revolution and is now known all over the world.

media.credit: Flan10 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Flan10

questions.description: A tower of bells so tall that nobody dares to ring the one at the bottom.
questions.question: In the Christmas carol “Campana sobre campana”, why do you look out of the window?
questions.answer: To see the Christ Child in his cradle
wrong_answers: To see the Three Wise Men arrive
To see the snow falling outside
To see the Star of Bethlehem
hints: The song is about what happened in Bethlehem.
Angels ring the bells to share some big news.
There's a newborn baby.
questions.fun_fact: It's a traditional carol from Andalusia, in Spain, that Mexicans sing at the posadas.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A star that everyone asks for its address, but it never answers.
questions.question: It's sung softly and slowly, and it compares a star to a diamond. Why do people sing “Estrellita, ¿dónde estás?”?
questions.answer: To lull a baby to sleep
hints: It's sung at night.
Moms sing it next to the crib.
It helps someone close their little eyes.
questions.fun_fact: Its tune is the same as “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”, and Mozart wrote variations on it.

media.credit: Chad Ajamian · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chad Ajamian

questions.description: A march so famous that even people who can't march stand up a little straighter.
questions.question: Genaro Codina wrote it in the 19th century, and people call it “the second national anthem.” Where do you hear the Marcha de Zacatecas?
hints: It's a military march.
Drum and bugle bands play it.
Think of September 16 and the flag ceremony at school.
questions.fun_fact: Its composer, Genaro Codina, was born in the city of Zacatecas itself.

media.credit: Martín Daniel Cordero Amézquita · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Martín Daniel Cordero Amézquita

questions.description: Before streaming, music went round and round… literally.
questions.question: Your grandparents' record player is spinning a record with “La patita” and “El ratón vaquero.” Who sings them?
hints: He started out on the radio in the 1930s.
His creator was born in Orizaba, Veracruz.
He's known as “el Grillito Cantor” (the Little Singing Cricket).
questions.fun_fact: Behind Cri-Cri was Francisco Gabilondo Soler, who wrote more than 200 children's songs.

media.credit: Joe Haupt from USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Haupt from USA

questions.description: A crown you win with jumping, clapping and balloons.
questions.question: Which singer is known in Mexico as “la Reina de los Niños” (the Queen of Kids)?
hints: She has been singing for children for more than 30 years.
At her concerts, kids and their parents jump around together.
Her name is a Russian woman’s name, like Olga or Natasha.
questions.fun_fact: Tatiana started out as a teen pop singer in the 1980s before she turned to children’s music.

media.credit: Kristen Wong · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kristen Wong

questions.description: The least punctual wolf in the forest: the kids are tired of waiting for him.
questions.question: In “Juguemos en el bosque”, the wolf answers: “I'm putting on my shirt,” then “my pants,” then “my shoes.” What is he doing?
hints: Think of what you do every morning before school.
Shirts, pants and shoes are all clothes.
When he's done, he'll be ready to go out.
questions.fun_fact: When the wolf is finally ready, he comes out to chase the kids, and everyone runs so he won't catch them.

media.credit: Sanzzu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sanzzu

questions.description: A spider more stubborn than you when you're told it's time for bed.
questions.question: You sing “Witsi witsi araña” while moving your fingers. After the rain washes the spider out, when does it climb up again?
hints: First the rain has to dry up.
It happens when the sky clears.
It's when it gets warm and everything shines.
questions.fun_fact: The English version, “Itsy Bitsy Spider,” is sung with the very same finger movements.

media.credit: Luc Viatour · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luc Viatour

questions.description: Shiny capes, colorful masks and a whole arena screaming: welcome to the ring.
questions.question: I was born as a movie character in 1952, and later a real wrestler brought me to life in the ring. A flying move bears my name worldwide. Who am I?
hints: In my first movie, the actor David Silva played me.
The wrestler Daniel García was the one who took me into the ring.
The move is called the “hurricanrana”.
questions.fun_fact: The “hurricanrana” is used today in wrestling all over the world, from Japan to the United States.

media.credit: EstrellaSuecia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EstrellaSuecia

questions.description: Before phone notifications, the news arrived at the top of someone's lungs.
questions.question: Next to the newsstand, the voceador (newspaper seller) shouts “¡Extra, extra!”. What does he mean?
questions.answer: A special edition is out with big news
wrong_answers: He's giving away a free magazine
The newsstand is about to close
hints: It's about what's inside the paper, not its price.
Something happened that everyone will want to know about.
It's a special newspaper printed because of one huge story.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, newspaper sellers are called “voceadores” because they shout out the headlines as loud as they can.

media.credit: Sharon Hahn Darlin · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sharon Hahn Darlin

questions.description: He gets here before you finish reading this sentence.
questions.question: I'm a little mouse with a huge sombrero, the fastest in all of Mexico, and I shout “¡Ándale, ándale, arriba, arriba!” Who am I?
hints: I appear in the Looney Tunes cartoons.
I always beat Sylvester the cat in a race.
My cousin is Slowpoke Rodriguez, the slowest mouse in Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: The 1955 short “Speedy Gonzales” won the Oscar for best animated short film.

media.credit: Dorothy Sherrill · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dorothy Sherrill

questions.description: Every great friendship starts with a good fight in the ring.
questions.question: You're watching an old movie where El Santo teams up with his most famous rival, born in Nuevo León. Who is he?
hints: Together they fought monsters and vampires on screen.
He never took off his mask in public.
His mask is the color of the sky, with silver trim.
questions.fun_fact: Blue Demon, whose real name was Alejandro Muñoz, also starred in his own comic book.

media.credit: Miguel Angel Omaña Rojas · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Miguel Angel Omaña Rojas

questions.description: With pencil, paper and plenty of stubbornness, he taught more than a few textbooks did.
questions.question: I was born in Zamora, Michoacán, in 1934, spent time in a seminary, then explained history, politics and healthy food with cartoons in cheap books. Who am I?
hints: My real name was Eduardo del Río.
I drew “Los Supermachos” and “Los Agachados.”
I signed my work with a single four-letter word.
questions.fun_fact: Rius published more than a hundred books, including “Marx for Beginners,” which was translated into many languages.

media.credit: Neropock · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Neropock

questions.description: Shiny capes, tall boots and masks in every color: that's how a ring idol gets dressed.
questions.question: Many Mexican luchadores, like El Santo, spent almost their whole careers without taking off their masks. Why did they wear them?
questions.answer: To keep who they were a secret
hints: Comic book heroes sometimes live two lives.
Outside the ring, they could walk down the street like any neighbor.
Like superheroes, nobody was supposed to see their real face or know their name.
questions.fun_fact: El Santo was buried wearing his mask, just as he had asked.

media.credit: Jonathan McIntosh · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jonathan McIntosh

questions.description: A wooden boy whose nose kept growing… and so did his director's trophy shelf.
questions.question: A stop-motion Pinocchio set in Mussolini's Italy won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2023. Which Mexican directed it?
hints: He's from Guadalajara.
He loves monsters and fantastic creatures.
He also directed “The Shape of Water”.
questions.fun_fact: The movie's puppets were animated frame by frame, moved just a tiny bit for each photo.

media.credit: Humbledaisy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Humbledaisy

questions.description: It makes more noise than a round of applause, and nobody ever tells it to be quiet.
questions.question: Look at the photo: this gets snapped shut in front of the camera before every take. What is it called?
hints: It has the scene and take numbers written on it.
An assistant holds it in front of the lens and calls out the scene before the director says “Action!”.
Its name sounds just like the noise it makes.
questions.fun_fact: The snap of the clapperboard is used later to sync the sound with the picture.

media.credit: Mattbr · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mattbr

questions.description: Building worlds is his job; winning awards is his hobby.
questions.question: Production designer Eugenio Caballero created the sets for three of these films. Which one is NOT his?
hints: He won the Oscar for Best Art Direction for a Guillermo del Toro film.
He worked with Cuarón on a black-and-white film.
The one that isn't his takes place almost entirely off Earth.
questions.fun_fact: For “Roma”, Eugenio Caballero's team rebuilt whole streets of 1970 Mexico City.

media.credit: Compiled by chris 論 (for the individual photographers see the sources section) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Compiled by chris 論 (for the individual photographers see the sources section)

questions.description: A movie where it seems nobody remembered to yell “cut.”
questions.question: You're watching Iñárritu's “Birdman,” which looks like one single unbroken shot inside a theater. What city is that theater in?
hints: The main character is an actor who wants to make it in serious theater.
He used to be famous for playing a winged superhero in the movies.
It's the city of the Statue of Liberty.
questions.fun_fact: The cinematographer of “Birdman,” Mexico's Emmanuel Lubezki, won three Oscars in a row.

media.credit: Runner1616 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Runner1616

questions.description: A little light that works overtime every November.
questions.question: On Día de Muertos, candles are lit on the ofrenda next to the photo of a loved one who has passed. By tradition, what are they for?
questions.answer: To guide the souls to the ofrenda
wrong_answers: To keep the ofrenda's food warm
To keep the flowers from wilting
hints: It has to do with the special visitors who arrive that night.
Those visitors come from very far away and need to find their way.
They do the same job a lighthouse does for ships.
questions.fun_fact: Many ofrendas also have a little path of cempasúchil petals, whose color and scent help the souls find their way.

media.credit: NPS Photo · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NPS Photo

questions.description: The plant that decorates garden walls and also works as a nurse.
questions.question: Its purple flowers are boiled, sweetened with honey and drunk warm. What do Mexican grandmas drink bugambilia (bougainvillea) tea for?
hints: People drink it mostly in the cold season.
It's a remedy for the throat and chest.
It calms what makes you go “hack, hack” all night.
questions.fun_fact: Bougainvillea is named after French explorer Louis-Antoine de Bougainville; the plant was described during his voyage around the world.

media.credit: Ввласенко · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ввласенко

questions.description: A house rule even stricter than no snacks before dinner.
questions.question: You've just spent all afternoon ironing and go to wash your hands. According to Mexican grandmothers, what will happen if you get them wet?
questions.answer: You'll get rheumatism in your hands
hints: The belief says the trouble is going from hot to cold.
The damage is felt in the joints.
It's a pain older people often feel in their bones.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors say wetting your hands after ironing doesn't cause rheumatism: arthritis has other causes, such as age or the immune system.

media.credit: Michael Slaten · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Slaten

questions.description: A movie so old that even the colors went on vacation.
questions.question: You're watching a Pedro Infante movie on TV and everything is in black and white. When do you think it was filmed?
hints: Your grandparents or great-grandparents could have seen it at the movies.
Back then, filming in color was very hard and expensive.
It isn't new, but it isn't from the time of castles either.
questions.fun_fact: In the Golden Age, almost all Mexican movies were in black and white; color only became common in the 1960s.

media.credit: Lowdown · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lowdown

questions.description: Here everyone hears about everything before it even happens.
questions.question: You walk into a vecindad like the one in “El Chavo del 8” or “Nosotros los pobres”. What will you NOT find there?
questions.answer: A swimming pool in every home
hints: Many families with little money live in a vecindad.
Almost everything is shared among the neighbors.
Look for what would be a luxury.
questions.fun_fact: Many vecindades in Mexico City’s historic center were once grand colonial mansions split up into rooms.

media.credit: Ehécatl Cabrera · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ehécatl Cabrera

questions.description: For anyone who just couldn't wait until nighttime to see a movie.
questions.question: I'm an early movie showing; my name comes from the French word for “morning”, and kids looked forward to me every Sunday. What am I?
hints: You didn't have to dress up to go.
It played before the evening shows.
In French, “matin” means “morning”.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican movie theaters had “permanencia voluntaria”: you paid for one ticket and could stay to watch several showings in a row.

media.credit: Warren LeMay from Cincinnati, OH, United States · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Warren LeMay from Cincinnati, OH, United States

questions.description: The spot in the house where the dog lives, the laundry sunbathes, and nobody knows who left that broken chair.
questions.question: In many Mexican homes, that's where you find the tinaco, the laundry hanging out to dry and sometimes even the dog. What is the azotea?
questions.answer: The flat roof of the house
hints: To get there, you almost always have to go up.
From there you can see the neighbors' houses.
It's at the very top of the house, above all the rooms.
questions.fun_fact: Flat roofs are so common in Mexico that the azotea works as a laundry room, storeroom, garden and even a ball court.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT

questions.description: The magic word you give away to any stranger with a full mouth.
questions.question: You walk past a table at a fonda where someone is eating. To be polite, in Mexico you say…
hints: You say it even if you don't know the person.
It's a good wish for their meal.
It means: may your food do you good.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it's common to say “provecho” even on your way out of a restaurant, to every table you pass.

media.credit: Karinadejesus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Karinadejesus

questions.description: Public enemy number one of shock absorbers and of the coffee in your cup holder.
questions.question: They're on streets all over Mexico, make your car jump if you drive fast and force drivers to slow down. What are they called?
hints: People or the government put them there on purpose.
They're like a small hill in the pavement.
Many are painted yellow so you can see them.
questions.fun_fact: In other countries, topes are called “lomos de burro” (donkey's backs), “muertos” (dead men) or “policías acostados” (lying-down policemen).

media.credit: DanTD · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DanTD

questions.description: A neighborhood where you need to have read the classics just to ask for directions.
questions.question: In this Mexico City colonia, streets are named Homero, Horacio, Aristóteles and Molière, and Avenida Masaryk has luxury shops. Which one is it?
hints: It's on the west side of the city.
It's right next to Chapultepec Park.
It's famous for its pricey restaurants and boutiques.
questions.fun_fact: Many of Polanco's streets are named after famous writers, philosophers and scientists from around the world.

media.credit: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Case

questions.description: The moment at a baptism when the smallest guests turn into Olympic athletes.
questions.question: Leaving a baptism in Mexico, children shout “¡bolo, bolo!” at the godfather. What does he throw into the air?
hints: The children race to pick it up off the ground.
Later they can spend it at the corner store.
It's money, but not bills.
questions.fun_fact: Today many godparents also hand out “bolos” as baptism keepsakes: little bags filled with candy.

media.credit: Iqmann · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Iqmann

questions.description: A cloud you can buy, but it vanishes the moment you bite it.
questions.question: It's sold in the park, the vendor carries it in little bags hanging from a long pole, and it melts in your mouth. What is it?
hints: It's sweet and very fluffy.
It's almost always pink or blue.
It's made by spinning hot sugar in a machine.
questions.fun_fact: A big cotton candy is made from just one or two spoonfuls of sugar.

media.credit: IcedCowboyCoffee · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: IcedCowboyCoffee

questions.description: A street snack so crunchy you can hear it from the next corner.
questions.question: Chicharrón preparado from street stalls is a crunchy rectangle topped with cream, cabbage, tomato and avocado. What is that chicharrón made of?
hints: Even though it's called chicharrón, it isn't pork.
It's sold dry and puffs up when it's fried.
It's the same main ingredient as bread and the tortillas of northern Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: Flour chicharrón is also called “duro,” and some stalls top it with cueritos (pickled pork skin).

media.credit: AlexandLeigh · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlexandLeigh

questions.description: The party with more waltz rehearsals than any wedding.
questions.question: At her XV años, like this quinceañera, her dad swaps her flat shoes for high heels. What does it mean?
questions.answer: She's no longer a little girl
hints: It has to do with growing up.
Along with the “last doll,” it marks a new stage of life.
It's a goodbye to childhood.
questions.fun_fact: At many XV años parties, the quinceañera dances a waltz with her chambelanes that they rehearse for weeks.

media.credit: Yuritzi Ramírez · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yuritzi Ramírez

questions.description: A neighbor so close it shares a border, tamales and even words.
questions.question: It's the most populous country in Central America, it borders Chiapas, and its name comes from Nahuatl. Which country is it?
hints: Its name is often translated as “place of many trees.”
Its national bird is the quetzal.
Its capital has almost the same name as the country.
questions.fun_fact: Besides Spanish, Guatemala recognizes 22 Mayan languages.

media.credit: EgorovaSvetlana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: EgorovaSvetlana

questions.description: Art so colorful that even a rainbow would ask permission to look at it.
questions.question: You're looking at a Huichol painting made of colored yarn. What material were the threads pressed into?
hints: It's a natural material that comes from an animal.
It softens in the heat of the sun.
It's made by the insects that make honey.
questions.fun_fact: The Wixárika (Huichol) people live mainly in the Sierra Madre Occidental, across Jalisco, Nayarit, Durango and Zacatecas.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: Three letters that have been working hard on Mexico's maps for centuries.
questions.question: It's at the end of Zapopan, Tuxpan and Ixtapan. In Nahuatl, what does the ending “-pan” do?
questions.answer: It marks a place: “on” or “on top of”
wrong_answers: It shows that something is very big
It shows that something happened long ago
hints: All three are names of places in Mexico.
It works like an English preposition.
It's the same idea as “the book is ___ the table.”
questions.fun_fact: Zapopan, in Jalisco, is often translated as “place among the zapotes,” after the trees of that fruit.

media.credit: Iqmann · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Iqmann

questions.description: A name so long that the Virgin preferred to call him “Juanito.”
questions.question: Juan Diego had a Nahuatl name: Cuauhtlatoatzin. Fill in what it means: “___ that speaks.”
hints: It's an animal on Mexico's coat of arms.
It's the same “cuauh” found in the name Cuauhtémoc.
It's a hunting bird that flies very high.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Diego was made a saint in 2002 and is considered the first Indigenous saint of the Americas.

media.credit: José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luiz

questions.description: A Guadalajara final with a taste of asado and mate.
questions.question: I'm Argentine and played for River Plate and Lazio. In 2017 I led Chivas past Tigres in the Clausura final. Who am I?
hints: After Chivas, I went to coach in MLS, in San Jose.
They call me “el Pelado” because of my shaved head.
My last name starts with A.
questions.fun_fact: With that title, Chivas reached 12 league championships and at the time tied América as the most successful club.

media.credit: Alejan98 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alejan98

questions.description: A trophy case that needed a few extra shelves in the fifties and sixties.
questions.question: How many league titles did Chivas's “Campeonísimo” team win between 1956 and 1965?
hints: It was the golden age of the “Rebaño Sagrado.”
They won almost every tournament that decade, but not all of them.
It's the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Campeonísimo, Chivas had never won the professional league: its first title came in the 1956–57 season.

media.credit: East Riding Archives · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: East Riding Archives

questions.description: A ship, a suitcase and a ball: that's how a national passion began.
questions.question: Estadio Hidalgo is in Pachuca, the “cradle of soccer” in Mexico. Who brought soccer there in the late 19th century?
hints: They came from abroad to work in the region's main industry.
They spoke English
Besides soccer, they brought pastes, the meat-filled pastries Pachuca is now famous for
questions.fun_fact: Pachuca, founded in 1901, proudly calls itself the oldest soccer club in Mexico.

media.credit: The Stadium Guide · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: The Stadium Guide

questions.description: His celebrations on the bench went around the world faster than the ball.
questions.question: Complete the nickname of the coach who wildly celebrated Mexico's goals at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil: Miguel “…” Herrera.
hints: As a player, he was a defender for Atlante.
His nickname is something nobody wants to find on their head.
It lives in hair and makes you itch.
questions.fun_fact: Herrera won two league titles with América, both in finals against Cruz Azul: Clausura 2013 and Apertura 2018.

questions.description: Mexico's short tournaments once changed names as often as you change jackets.
questions.question: They ran from 1996 to 2002, Santos Laguna won the first one, and then the names changed. What were these short tournaments called?
hints: They have to do with the weather
They are seasons of the year
One of them was played around Christmas time

media.credit: Peter Glaser baraida · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Peter Glaser baraida

questions.description: An Andalusian who swapped gazpacho for Monterrey's cabrito.
questions.question: When Sergio Ramos joined Rayados in 2025, he picked a shirt number honoring his famous goal in the 2014 Champions League final. Which one?
hints: It's a two-digit number

It was a stoppage-time header against Atlético in Lisbon

media.credit: Hafid (HDavilaMedia) Davila hafiddavila · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hafid (HDavilaMedia) Davila hafiddavila

questions.description: A tournament where the neighbors to the north and to the south fight over the same trophy.
questions.question: This tournament brings together clubs from North and Central America and the Caribbean, has been played since 1962, and its champion goes to the Club World Cup. Which country has won it most?

América and Cruz Azul are among the biggest winners.
questions.fun_fact: From 2006 to 2021, every edition of the tournament was won by a Mexican club.

media.credit: Tomofumi Kitano · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tomofumi Kitano

questions.description: A hold that turns your opponent into the world's most uncomfortable horse.
questions.question: In “la de a caballo,” the wrestler sits on the back of a face-down opponent and pulls their head back. What is it for?
questions.answer: To make the opponent give up

To pull off the opponent's mask

Bending the back like that hurts a lot.
The opponent ends up tapping the mat or shouting “ya!” (enough!).

media.credit: Roberto Murillo Medina · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Roberto Murillo Medina

questions.description: A circus where nobody wants a front-row seat.
questions.question: You're at an AAA show and they announce Los Psycho Circus. What are its wrestlers dressed as?
hints: They are three masked wrestlers who usually fight together in trios matches.
Their masks are in loud colors and are a little scary.
Each of their names ends in the English word for a circus performer with a red nose.
questions.fun_fact: Psycho Clown, the most famous of the trio, is the son of the luchador Brazo de Plata, known as Super Porky.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: Colorful masks, shouting from the stands and a referee who never sees anything.
questions.question: In Mexican lucha libre, what is a “técnico”?
questions.answer: The clean wrestler who follows the rules
wrong_answers: The wrestler who always fights unmasked
The heaviest wrestler on the card
The wrestler who trains the rookies

media.author: Chrkl

questions.description: The place where you learned that modeling clay is not a snack.
questions.question: In Mexico, when do you go to kínder?
hints: You go when you're very little.

It's the first school you ever go to.
questions.fun_fact: The word kínder comes from the German Kindergarten, which means “garden of children”, just like the Mexican name jardín de niños.

media.credit: woodleywonderworks · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: woodleywonderworks

questions.description: The hero of every school presentation made the night before.
questions.question: It's thick, stiff paper that comes in colored sheets, and the teacher asks for it to make presentation posters. What is it called?
hints: It's thicker than a normal sheet but thinner than cardboard.
It stays standing if you lean it against the board.
Its name sounds like a tiny “cartón”.
questions.fun_fact: The word cartulina comes from the Italian “cartolina”, which in Italy today means postcard.

questions.question: Complete it: CONALEP is the Colegio Nacional de Educación…
hints: It is a high-school-level school.
It was founded in the late 1970s.
The P and the T at the end are your clue.
questions.fun_fact: CONALEP was created in 1978 to train the technicians that Mexican industry needed.

media.author: National Library of Ireland on The Commons

questions.description: Six years of times tables and then… time to grow up!
questions.question: In Mexico, when you finish sixth grade of primaria, which school do you move on to?
hints: It's the school that comes right after.
You're there from about age 12 to 15.
Its name sounds like “second”.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, secundaria lasts three years and has been compulsory since 1993.

media.author: Personal Creations

questions.description: The earliest lines in the colonia, bag and card in hand.
questions.question: For decades, Liconsa has sold one product at a low price to millions of Mexican families. Which one?
hints: It's sold in its own little shops, in bags.
Registered families get a card to buy their weekly share.
Its outlets are called lecherías.
questions.fun_fact: Liconsa milk is fortified with iron, zinc and vitamins to fight anemia in children.

media.credit: Raul21940 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Raul21940

questions.description: The photo where we all look like we just woke up.

hints: You have to renew it about every ten years.
It used to be issued by the IFE.
It gets marked when you go to the casilla.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico started issuing the voter card with a photo in 1992.

media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: The school where you decide what you want to be when you grow up… or at least you try.
questions.question: In Mexico, you've finished secundaria and want to go to university. Which school do you still need?
hints: It usually lasts two or three years.
When you finish it, you take the university entrance exam.
Its name says it gets you ready for university.
questions.fun_fact: UNAM's Escuela Nacional Preparatoria was founded in 1867 in the old Colegio de San Ildefonso.

media.author: Gary Todd

questions.description: A household tragedy right in the middle of your shower.

hints: The cylinder is made of metal and sits on the azotea or in the patio.
The water heater uses it too.
It's sold from a truck that drives down the street announcing itself.
questions.fun_fact: LP gas has no smell of its own: a strong odor is added on purpose so you notice if there's a leak.

questions.description: A nickname people give you without asking, and sometimes it doesn't even fit.
questions.question: You're on the street and hear someone shout “¡Ey, flaco!”. Literally, what kind of person are they calling?
hints: It's about the body, not the personality.

It's someone with hardly any belly.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, many people call their partner “flaca” or “flaco” as a pet name, even if they aren't thin at all.

questions.description: Two words parents hate to hear when they ask about homework.
questions.question: If a Mexican teen says “me vale”, what do they mean?
hints: It has nothing to do with money or prices.

It's what you answer when something means nothing at all to you.
questions.fun_fact: “Me vale” gave Mexico the word “valemadrismo”, for an attitude where nothing matters to you.

media.author: Lance Cpl. Jackeline M. Perez Rivera

questions.description: Cartoons have their own dictionary of shouts, and this word is on almost every page.

wrong_answers: To greet someone from far away
To ask someone for a match
hints: It's a word that slips out without thinking.
For example, when your ice cream falls on the floor.
It takes the place of a word you shouldn't say in front of kids.
questions.fun_fact: Many mild exclamations like “¡chispas!” or “¡rayos!” were born so people wouldn't use bad words in front of the family.

It's something that rubs you the wrong way or looks awful.
questions.fun_fact: To say something is really bad, Mexicans pile it on with “gachísimo”.

media.author: Alison wood

You answer it with something like “good, and you?”.
questions.fun_fact: If someone in Mexico tells you something “es un rollo”, they mean it's long, complicated or boring.

A volcanic stone that glows when heated

The front flippers are much bigger and do almost all the work when swimming.
It's an even number, smaller than five.
questions.fun_fact: Female sea turtles often return to lay their eggs on the same beach where they hatched.

questions.description: The unluckiest days of the year: even grandma wouldn't go out to the corner store.
questions.question: As an ancient Maya, you wouldn't bathe or leave home during Uayeb. How many days did it last at the end of the 365-day year?
hints: The other months of the year had 20 days each.
There were 18 of those months.
Do the math: 365 minus 360.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica also had 5 unlucky days at the end of their year: they called them nemontemi.

hints: He is part of life in the Maya farming villages of Yucatán.
There are still some today in the Maya villages of Yucatán.
His name in Maya means roughly “the one who knows” or “the one who does”.
questions.fun_fact: The crystal stone the h-men uses to tell the future is called a sastún.

questions.description: A serpent that shows up on time every year and never needs an entry ticket.

hints: It only appears on sunny afternoons.
If a cloud comes by, the serpent disappears.
They are triangles the Sun makes as it hits the corners of the pyramid.
questions.fun_fact: Every equinox, thousands of people dressed in white go to Chichén Itzá to watch Kukulcán come down and soak up its energy.

From 17 to 20 is only a few pesos.
They have to give you back 3 pesos.
questions.fun_fact: At many tienditas, if they're out of change, they make up the difference with a candy or a piece of gum.

hints: For gold, karats don't measure weight.

The Centenario got a bit of copper to make it tougher.
questions.fun_fact: The Centenario was first minted in 1921 to celebrate 100 years since Mexico's independence was won.

It's worked out as a percentage.
The usual amount is between 10 and 15%.
questions.fun_fact: In supermarkets, the kids and older folks who bag your groceries are called “cerillitos,” and they work for tips.

Its purity matches the most famous silver investment coins from other countries.
Its purity is written as “.999”.

hints: Fans call the team by a nickname that comes from its colors.

It's the color of a nopal cactus.
questions.fun_fact: Estadio Azteca is the first stadium to host matches at three World Cups: 1970, 1986 and 2026.

The eagle from the coat of arms sits on that stripe.
It's the color of snow.
questions.fun_fact: The three stripes of the Mexican flag are vertical and exactly the same width.

Hidalgo and Morelos are among the most famous.

I came after Cuitláhuac.
A borough (alcaldía) of Mexico City bears my name.
questions.fun_fact: In Nahuatl, the name Cuauhtémoc means “descending eagle.”

Years later I became governor of Morelos.
The move is named after me: the “cuauhtemiña”.
questions.fun_fact: Cuauhtémoc Blanco showed off the “cuauhtemiña” at the 1998 World Cup against South Korea.

questions.fun_fact: Dr. Atl watched the Paricutín volcano being born in 1943 and painted it again and again.

There are six pairs of strings.

It hangs above the main balcony, facing the Zócalo.

hints: The Mexica spoke it in Tenochtitlan.

The word “Mexico” comes from it too.
questions.fun_fact: “Chicle” (gum), “cacahuate” (peanut) and “papalote” (kite) also come from Nahuatl.

questions.fun_fact: Chicle is also a tree resin, but people chew that one instead of burning it.

Its name has just one syllable and an apostrophe.

The odd name out belonged to a daughter of Moctezuma.
questions.fun_fact: Her name gave Mexico the word “malinchista”, used for someone who prefers anything foreign.

Frida Kahlo painted herself in this dress many times.

The first word of its name means “little female pig.”
questions.fun_fact: Achiote, which gives the dish its red color, comes from the seeds of a shrub native to the Americas.

Some friars promised to stay behind as prisoners so others could go free.

They're cooked a lot like spinach.

questions.question: The bolillo is long, crusty outside and soft inside. According to Mexican tradition, what is eating a piece of one good for?

It's given to someone who looks pale and shaken.
There's a saying: “un bolillo para el…”.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico people even say “un bolillo para el susto” after a big scare during a soccer game.

media.author: Magdachan23

questions.description: In Mexico, the food comes with its own edible helper.
questions.question: You're eating beans and there's no cutlery. In Mexico, a folded piece of tortilla works as a…
hints: It's something you use at the table every day.
It's used to lift food.
You use it to eat soup.
questions.fun_fact: A tortilla folded for eating is sometimes called “the Mexican spoon,” because you eat it along with whatever it scoops up.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: A Christmas tradition where breaking the dishes is good manners.
questions.question: In which city do people throw and smash the clay plate after eating a buñuelo with honey in December, for good luck?
hints: It's a city in southern Mexico.
The Noche de Rábanos is also celebrated there.
It's famous for its mole negro and the Guelaguetza.
questions.fun_fact: The Noche de Rábanos (Night of the Radishes) is held every December 23 with figures carved from giant radishes.

media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A present you unwrap with an empty stomach.
questions.question: You're in Oaxaca and you unwrap an Oaxacan tamal with mole negro. What is it wrapped in?
hints: It's not what Mexico City's tamal verde comes wrapped in.
It's a big, green, shiny leaf.
It comes from a plant that grows a yellow fruit.
questions.fun_fact: The banana leaf is passed over a flame before use so it softens and doesn't tear.

media.credit: Bluerasberry · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bluerasberry

questions.description: The fair snack you walk around holding hands with, like in the movies.
questions.question: At the fair it's sold on a stick, coated in fried batter and topped with ketchup and mustard. What's inside a classic banderilla?
hints: It's salty, not sweet.
It's meat, and it comes already cooked in a package.
It's long and pink.
questions.fun_fact: In the US, the banderilla is known as a “corn dog,” because its batter is made with cornmeal.

media.author: victorherrera

questions.description: In boxing the punches hit hard, but the abbreviations hit even harder.
questions.question: In boxing, a “technical knockout,” or TKO, gives a fighter the win. What does it mean?
questions.answer: The referee stops the fight: a boxer can't go on
wrong_answers: The winner knocked him out with a punch to the neck
The judges give the win on points
The opponent missed the weigh-in time
hints: Nobody has to count to ten.
It happens when a boxer can no longer defend himself properly.
The person who decides is the one walking between the two fighters.
questions.fun_fact: It is also a technical knockout when a boxer's corner throws in the towel to give up.

media.credit: Micheal Kaluba · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Micheal Kaluba

questions.description: Cookies so brave they jump into the glass of milk all by themselves.
questions.question: What are these little cookies called?
hints: They're tiny, and lots of them come in one bag.
Each one has a different shape.
You might find an elephant or a lion among them.
questions.fun_fact: Animal-shaped cookies were already being baked in England in the 1800s.

media.author: Willis Lam

questions.description: A cookie that dresses up in pink to go to the party.
questions.question: Sponch are Marinela cookies with a pink or white marshmallow on top. What is that marshmallow covered with?
hints: It feels a little scratchy on your tongue.
It comes from a fruit with a very hard shell.
It comes from the hairy fruit that grows on palm trees.
questions.fun_fact: The marshmallow is named after a plant, the marsh mallow, whose root was once used to make it.

media.credit: Mk2010 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mk2010

questions.description: The one neighbor everyone runs from when he shows up: he’s here to collect the rent.
questions.question: The owner of the vecindad is called Señor Barriga. What part of the body is a “barriga”?
hints: It’s a part of the body.
That’s where you feel it when you’re hungry.
Your navel sits right in the middle of it.
questions.fun_fact: Édgar Vivar played Señor Barriga and also his son Ñoño.

media.credit: Adam Jones, Ph.D. · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Jones, Ph.D.

questions.description: A visitor to the vecindad who never shows up without her best friend made of rags.
questions.question: I'm Doña Florinda's niece and Quico's cousin, I talk with a nasal voice and always carry my doll Serapia. Who am I?
hints: I'm played by Florinda Meza, the same actress who plays my aunt.
I go to school with Profesor Jirafales.
My name is also Mexican slang for “posh” or “fancy.”
questions.fun_fact: Florinda Meza played both Doña Florinda and her niece, la Popis.

media.credit: Anne Norman · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Anne Norman

questions.description: An actor so tall he had to duck to get into any character.
questions.question: Which of these characters was NOT played by Rubén Aguirre?
hints: Rubén Aguirre played the vecindad's famous teacher.
That character was played by Chespirito himself.
He's a very old doctor who gets angry if you call him old.
questions.fun_fact: Rubén Aguirre was about 1.96 m (6 ft 5 in) tall, which is why his character is called Jirafales, from “jirafa” (giraffe).

media.credit: Nesnad · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nesnad

questions.description: The Kings have to stick their noses where nobody else dares.
questions.question: On the night of January 5, Mexican children leave out their shoes. Before going to sleep, what do they usually put inside?
questions.answer: Their letter to the Three Kings
hints: They get it ready right before going to bed.
The Kings check it before leaving the presents.
In it they say how well they behaved and which toys they want.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, some children also tie their letter to a helium balloon and let it go, so it flies all the way to the Kings.

media.credit: Maksym Kozlenko · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Maksym Kozlenko

questions.description: A manger with more visitors than Grandma's house at Christmas.
questions.question: You're setting up the nacimiento and the Niño Dios is already in his manger. Who does NOT belong there?
hints: Three of them are part of the story of Bethlehem.
One arrives by sleigh from the North Pole.
The one dressed in red who says “Ho, ho, ho.”
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican homes the nacimiento stays up until February 2, the Día de la Candelaria (Candlemas).

media.credit: WILRIT - Wilson Fernandez · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: WILRIT - Wilson Fernandez

questions.description: The nativity decoration that spends all Christmas hanging from the ceiling without complaining.
questions.question: In a nativity scene, the angel hangs above the stable. In the story of Bethlehem, what did the angel do that night?
hints: It happened the same night Jesus was born.
It appeared in the fields, at night.
It told some men looking after sheep that the Baby had been born.
questions.fun_fact: In many nativity scenes, the angel holds a ribbon with the Latin words “Gloria in excelsis Deo”.

media.author: WILRIT - Wilson Fernandez

questions.description: Your reward for singing outside in the cold, begging for a place to stay.
questions.question: At the end of a posada, you get a little bag called an “aguinaldo”. What is usually inside?
hints: Kids can't wait to get it after the singing.
It may have peanuts and a mandarin orange.
It has colorful sugar candies and other sweets.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, “aguinaldo” is also the extra year-end pay that workers get in December.

media.credit: José Sanchez / José Guadalupe Posada · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Sanchez / José Guadalupe Posada

questions.description: At the fonda, hunger is the boss, and sometimes the menu speaks in code.
questions.question: At a fonda in Mexico City, you order a huarache with beans, salsa and cheese. What do you get?
questions.answer: A long corn-dough base with toppings
wrong_answers: A round sweet bun with a sugar crust
A tamale wrapped in a banana leaf
A tortilla soup with pasilla chile
hints: It's an antojito made of masa, like sopes and tlacoyos.
Its name comes from its shape.
It's flat and oval, like the sole of a sandal.
questions.fun_fact: The huarache as a dish is said to have been born in Mexico City in the 1930s, at a stand by the La Viga canal.

media.credit: Daniela Magallán Ramírez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniela Magallán Ramírez

questions.description: The biggest living room in the country, and it doesn't even have a couch.
questions.question: Look at the photo: what do people call this huge square in the center of Mexico City?
hints: It hosts concerts, parades and the September 15 celebration.
The Cathedral and the National Palace stand right next to it.
Its official name is Plaza de la Constitución.
questions.fun_fact: It's called the Zócalo because for years it only had the base (in Spanish, “zócalo”) of an Independence monument that was never finished.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A garment that takes months to embroider and two seconds to win over Frida Kahlo.
questions.question: Look at this embroidery: which traditional garment of Mexico's Indigenous women is it?
hints: Frida Kahlo wore it in many of her self-portraits.
It's a blouse or tunic without long sleeves, with an opening for the head.
It's widely worn in Oaxaca, Chiapas and Yucatán, and its name comes from Nahuatl.
questions.fun_fact: In many towns, the designs on a huipil show which community the person wearing it comes from.

media.credit: Photo: Nosferattus; garment: unknown · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Photo: Nosferattus; garment: unknown

questions.description: When Mexico scores, the whole city knows exactly where to go and shout.
questions.question: When Mexico's national team wins, fans go to celebrate at a monument on Reforma. Complete its name: the Angel of…
hints: The monument is a column topped by a golden figure with wings.
It honors the heroes who fought against Spain.
It's celebrated every September 16.
questions.fun_fact: The golden Angel statue fell during the 1957 earthquake and had to be restored.

media.credit: Kajuy-FUO-3365 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kajuy-FUO-3365

questions.description: One signature in Veracruz that saved Mexico several more chapters of war.
questions.question: You're at the Portal de Zevallos in Córdoba, Veracruz, where the treaties recognizing Mexico's independence were signed. In what year?
hints: It was in the early 19th century, when Mexico stopped being New Spain.
They were signed by Agustín de Iturbide and Juan O'Donojú.
That same year, the Army of the Three Guarantees marched into Mexico City.
questions.fun_fact: The Treaties of Córdoba were signed on August 24, 1821, but Spain didn't accept them until years later.

media.credit: Rodolfo corona ramírez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rodolfo corona ramírez

questions.description: A feathered fellow who wakes up the whole ranch, mariachi band included.
questions.question: He's a charro rooster from Jalisco with a huge sombrero, and in 1944 he sang in a Disney film with Donald Duck and a Brazilian parrot. What's his name?
hints: The film is called “The Three Caballeros.”
His parrot friend is named José Carioca.
His last name sounds like the guns he fires into the air when he gets excited.
questions.fun_fact: In the story, his full name is Panchito Romero Miguel Junípero Francisco Quintero González III.

media.credit: Elizjorge · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Elizjorge

questions.description: A colonial building that today can't take anything seriously.
questions.question: The Museo de la Caricatura, on Calle de Donceles in Mexico City's historic center, is in a colonial building. What was it originally?
hints: It was founded in the early 17th century.
A rich man founded it with money he left in his will.
Young people who couldn't afford their studies lived there.
questions.fun_fact: The museum is run by the Sociedad Mexicana de Caricaturistas, the guild of Mexico's cartoonists, the “moneros”.

media.credit: José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luiz

questions.description: Pow! Zap! This question comes with sound effects included.
questions.question: Comics are full of onomatopoeias, words that imitate sounds. Which of these groups are NOT onomatopoeias?
hints: An onomatopoeia sounds just like the noise it imitates.
A punch, a rooster or a clock sound like this in comics.
Look for the words you say to cheer someone on or when you're surprised, not to imitate a noise.
questions.fun_fact: Dogs don't “say” the same thing in every language: in English they bark “woof” and in Japanese “wan wan”.

media.credit: Cpl. Brittany A. James · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cpl. Brittany A. James

questions.description: A character who loves coming out of his shell… but not getting into the frying pan.
questions.question: I'm a brave egg from a Mexican animated movie, and my best friend is a strip of bacon named Willy. Who am I?
hints: In my world, food talks and goes on adventures.
My name has only four letters, and I'm a boy, not a girl.
My name rhymes with “photo”.
questions.fun_fact: Willy the bacon was voiced by Mexican actor and comedian Carlos Espejel.

media.credit: Krzysztof Golik · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Krzysztof Golik

questions.description: The jewel that took on the colors of a sunset over the semi-desert.
questions.question: It's a gem that flashes many colors, ranges from yellow to red and is mined in Querétaro. What is it?
hints: Tequisquiapan, in Querétaro, is famous for selling it.
It has a little water trapped inside.
Its name brings flames to mind.
questions.fun_fact: Opal holds water inside, so it can crack if it dries out too much.

media.credit: Carlos Valenzuela · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Valenzuela

questions.description: Grandma's hug, served in a deep bowl.
questions.question: Look at this chicken and vegetable soup. When does Grandma make it for you as a remedy?
hints: It's when you're stuck in bed and don't feel like doing anything.
Here come the runny nose and the sneezing.
It's that illness with chills, a cough and a stuffy nose.
questions.fun_fact: A study from 2000 found that chicken soup may slightly reduce swelling in the nose and throat.

media.author: El Gran Dee

questions.description: A remedy that sounds like you're drowning on purpose.

hints: Every home has it in the kitchen.
It isn't sweet.
The sea tastes like this.
questions.fun_fact: Salty water draws fluid out of a swollen throat and brings the swelling down a little.

media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: An illness so strange that its cure looks like a circus act.
