hints: It isn't a tummy illness or one caused by a look.
It has to do with the baby's head.
“Mollera” is what people call the soft spot on a baby's head.
questions.fun_fact: For doctors, a sunken soft spot can be a sign of dehydration, so the baby needs fluids and a trip to the doctor.

media.credit: Toshiyuki IMAI from Kyoto, Japan · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Toshiyuki IMAI from Kyoto, Japan

questions.description: A candy that smiles even without lips.
questions.question: Look at this sugar skull. On a Day of the Dead ofrenda, who is it placed for?
questions.answer: For family members who have died
wrong_answers: For kids who have a birthday
hints: It's a way to remember someone who is no longer here.
Their photos go on the ofrenda too.
They're the grandparents, great-grandparents and other loved ones who are gone.
questions.fun_fact: Alfeñique, the sugar technique used to make the little skulls, came to Mexico from Spain in colonial times.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: The favorite decoration of every hopeful shopkeeper.
questions.question: In a shop you see a curved, cone-shaped charm hanging up, filled with corn, beans, rice and coins and renewed every year. What is it called?
wrong_answers: The sábila with a red ribbon
hints: It's a very old symbol, much older than Mexico.
It also appears on the coats of arms of several countries.
Its name promises you'll never be short of anything.
questions.fun_fact: In Greek mythology it was the horn of the goat Amalthea, who nursed the baby Zeus.

media.author: Adam Jones

questions.description: The thing you really wear brand new on December 31, and nobody sees it.

questions.answer: Red for love and yellow for money
wrong_answers: Yellow for love and red for money
Blue for love and black for money
Purple for love and brown for money
hints: This custom is also followed in other Latin American countries.
Both colors are warm, like fire.
One is the color of hearts and the other the color of gold.
questions.fun_fact: In Brazil the tradition is different: people dress in white to welcome the new year.

media.author: Eneas De Troya from Mexico City, México

questions.answer: At the corner of the table
wrong_answers: At the head of the table
hints: It's a spot on the table itself.
It's at the edge of the table, but it isn't the place of honor.
It's where the table comes to a point.
questions.fun_fact: The same belief exists in Russia: there, too, they say whoever sits at the corner of the table won't marry for seven years.

media.author: Hans Bernhard Schwerin

questions.description: A syrup that comes from the pantry, not the pharmacy.
questions.question: For a cough, Grandma gives you a spoonful of honey with a few drops of a green, very sour fruit. Which one?
hints: It's small and round.
You squeeze it over tacos.
It's so sour that biting into one makes you scrunch up your face.
questions.fun_fact: Honey should never be given to babies under one year old, so this remedy is for older kids.

media.credit: Ruffiana · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ruffiana

questions.description: A warning from Grandma: the sky has its own rules of good manners.
questions.question: In Mexico they say that if you point at a rainbow, you'll get a “mezquino”. What is a mezquino?
hints: It shows up on your skin.
It's a small hard bump that sometimes appears on your hands.
A virus causes it, and a dermatologist can remove it.
questions.fun_fact: Warts are caused by a virus that spreads through touch, not by rainbows.

media.credit: iMahesh · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: iMahesh

questions.description: A song so sweet it could sweeten even a cup of café de olla.
questions.question: You hear Pedro Infante sing “Amorcito corazón” in the movie “Nosotros los pobres”. In which decade did it come out?
hints: Your great-grandparents could have seen it at the movies when they were young.
It’s in black and white, like almost all films of the Golden Age.
It came out about three years after the end of World War II.
questions.fun_fact: “Amorcito corazón” was written by Manuel Esperón and Pedro de Urdimalas, and in the movie Pepe el Toro sings it to Celia, “la Chorreada.”

media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: Dancing hips that arrived in Mexico on a one-way ticket.
questions.question: This is Ninón Sevilla, queen of the rumberas of Mexican cinema. In which country was she born?
hints: She wasn't born in Mexico, though she made her whole film career there.
Her country is an island in the Caribbean.
She was born in the capital famous for its Malecón and its old classic cars.
questions.fun_fact: French critics such as François Truffaut were big admirers of Ninón Sevilla's cabaret films.

questions.description: Soccer nicknames are like grade-school nicknames: one of them snuck in where it doesn't belong.

The odd one out belongs to a team from Querétaro.
questions.fun_fact: Puebla is called “La Franja” because of the blue band that runs diagonally across its white jersey.

media.author: Alejan98

questions.description: A fan group that sings so loud the neighbors don't even bother turning on the TV.

They're called the Águilas.
questions.fun_fact: La Monumental is one of the biggest and best-known supporters' groups in Mexican soccer.

media.author: Krzysztof Popławski

questions.description: Three kept their secret under the fabric, and one showed his face from day one.
questions.question: Which of these legendary luchadores did NOT wear a mask?
hints: He won many bet matches against masked wrestlers and for opponents' hair.

His ring name includes the Spanish word for an animal that barks.

questions.description: Maya architects nobody ever told that less is more.
questions.question: Plain walls below, stone mosaics above, full of masks of the god Chaac: it's the style of Uxmal, Sayil and Labná. What is it called?
hints: It is found in the hilly part of Yucatán.
Its Maya name means “hills” or “hill country.”
A tourist route with this name runs from Uxmal to Labná.
questions.fun_fact: In this style, facade stones were cut like puzzle pieces and set onto a core of Maya concrete.

media.author: edenpictures

questions.description: The social media profile of Maya kings: a picture, a date and lots of bragging.
questions.question: It's a tall stone slab that stood in plazas, carved with a ruler and dates in glyphs. Calakmul has over a hundred. What is it?
hints: It always stands upright, like a little wall all on its own.
It often had a low, round stone in front of it.
Its name comes from Greek, and it's also used for monuments in Egypt and Greece.
questions.fun_fact: Calakmul, in Campeche, is the Maya city with the most known stelae: about 120.

media.author: Oogstweg

questions.description: A calendar that's no help at all for knowing when the quincena gets paid.
questions.question: The tzolkin, the sacred Maya calendar, lasts 260 days, was used for ceremonies and naming babies, and is still used today. How is it made up?

Each day pairs a number from 1 to 13 with a sign such as Imix or Ik.

media.author: Internet Archive Book Images

questions.description: A field where not even Chicharito could score with his feet.

questions.fun_fact: The court has a famous echo: someone speaking at one end can be heard at the other.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: It was bouncing thousands of years before sneakers were invented.

They are called the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica.
One of their great cities was La Venta, and they carved jade figures with jaguar features.
questions.fun_fact: Mesoamericans mixed latex from the rubber tree with the juice of a vine to make their balls bounce better.

media.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

questions.description: A pyramid with a secret basement and a staircase straight out of a movie.
questions.question: The pyramid of the Temple of the Inscriptions in Palenque has as many stepped levels as the Maya underworld had layers. How many is that?

It's 3 squared.
questions.fun_fact: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spent about four years clearing the hidden staircase that leads to Pakal's tomb, which he found in 1952.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT

questions.description: You're taking a dip right in the middle of the dictionary.
questions.question: You're swimming in a cenote in Yucatán. Which people does the word “cenote” come from?
hints: They wrote with glyphs and created a very precise calendar.
The original word is ts'ono'ot.
They are the same people who built Chichén Itzá.
questions.fun_fact: Almost 800,000 people speak Yucatec Maya today: it's the second most spoken Indigenous language in Mexico, after Nahuatl.

media.author: Shinya Suzuki

questions.description: Payday comes and the money appears like magic… on a little piece of plastic.
questions.question: Your job sets it up for you, you use it at the ATM and the supermarket, and your pay lands on it every quincena. What is a “tarjeta de nómina”?

questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it's very common to be paid by the quincena: once in the middle of the month and again at the end.

media.credit: Lou Stejskal · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lou Stejskal

questions.description: Take it home today and suffer just a little each month.
questions.question: You buy a 6,000-peso TV on a credit card at 12 months interest-free. How much do you pay each month?

Divide the price by the number of months.
It's exactly half of 1,000.

media.author: Nikolina Šepić

questions.description: A question about counting the days, just like every student does in June.
questions.question: You check the SEP school calendar. About how many days of class are in a school year?
hints: There are summer, winter and Holy Week vacations.
Saturdays and Sundays don't count.
It's about 38 weeks of Monday to Friday.
questions.fun_fact: The SEP was founded in 1921, and its first secretary was José Vasconcelos.

media.credit: Mercedes Steph · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mercedes Steph

questions.description: Eighteen characters that say more about you than your horoscope.
questions.question: It has 18 characters, it's on your birth certificate, and schools ask for it when you sign up. What is the CURP for?
hints: You get it when you're still a baby.
It's made from letters of your name, your date of birth and the place where you were born.
The U in its acronym stands for “Única” (unique).
questions.fun_fact: In your CURP, the 11th character is H or M (hombre or mujer) depending on your sex, and the next two show the state where you were born.

media.credit: Friedrich Haag · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Friedrich Haag

questions.description: This phrase shoots out every time someone shares the gossip of the year.
questions.question: You shout me when someone tells you something unbelievable. I sound like I'm calling them a liar, but I only show surprise. What expression am I?
hints: You hear it all the time among Mexican teens.
It's a close cousin of “¡No manches!”.
Its verb is the thing Thomas Edison was famous for doing.
questions.fun_fact: “¡No inventes!” works for good and bad surprises alike: winning a prize or a pop quiz.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A nickname that saves a lot of money on shampoo.
questions.question: In Mexico, what fond nickname do people give someone with no hair at all?
hints: The nickname describes the head.
Newborn babies sometimes get called this too.
It sounds like the word “pelo” (hair) with a bigger ending.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexican nicknames, “chino” has nothing to do with China: it's what you call someone with curly hair.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.description: Your ice cream just hit the ground, and this is the only word that comes out.
questions.question: When something goes wrong or surprises you, people say “¡híjole!” all the time. In which country is this word so typical?
hints: It's a country in the Americas.
It shares a border with a much bigger neighbor to the north.
Its capital is one of the biggest cities in the world.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Híjole!” comes from “hijo” (son), and you can stretch it out as long as you like: “¡híjoleeee!”.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: A word so tiny it fits right into the moment you remember you forgot your homework.
questions.question: It's super short, you say it when you drop your taco or forget something, and it saves you from saying a bad word. Which word is it?
hints: You say it when something small goes wrong.
Many people use it to avoid a ruder word that starts the same way.
Its cousin is “¡chale!”.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico “¡Aguas!” means “Watch out!”, and people say it comes from the days when dirty water was thrown out of windows.

questions.description: A chilango phrase that sounds like someone just greeted their aunt in the middle of the street.
questions.question: It's said when you're fed up, it's classic Mexico City slang, and it ends with the nickname for women named Soledad. What expression is it?
hints: You use it to ask someone to stop doing something.
It's said in a tired voice, stretching out the last word.
It starts with “ya” and ends with a name.
questions.fun_fact: “Chole” is the traditional nickname for Soledad, just as “Lupe” is for Guadalupe and “Chucho” for Jesús.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: An air conditioner with heavenly powers that always shows up at just the right moment.
questions.question: Which TV show is the famous “vientito” from, the little breeze that blows when a miracle is about to happen?
wrong_answers: Mujer, casos de la vida real
hints: It is a Televisa show that has been on the air since 2008.
Each episode tells a different story about a problem that seems to have no solution.
After the vientito, a white flower appears.
questions.fun_fact: The vientito became so famous that there are thousands of memes and parodies of it on social media.

media.author: w_lemay

questions.description: A song so good that a whole telenovela took its name.
questions.question: Which Mexican singer-songwriter wrote “Te sigo amando,” the theme song of the telenovela with the same name?
hints: He's one of the most famous songwriters in Mexican music.
He wrote “Amor eterno” and “Querida.”
He was nicknamed “El Divo de Juárez.”
questions.fun_fact: Juan Gabriel wrote more than 1,500 songs, and many of them were recorded by other artists.

media.author: A S M Jobaer

questions.description: The moment in a telenovela when every relative suddenly becomes very loving.
questions.question: The notary arrives at the mansion and the whole family sits in silence. Finish the cliché: “Now begins the reading of the…”
hints: It decides who gets the fortune.
There is almost always a surprise: someone nobody expected gets everything.
It's the paper where someone writes down what each relative inherits.
questions.fun_fact: In many telenovelas, a surprise inheritance is what turns the poor girl into a millionaire.

media.author: ElooKoN

questions.description: Twelve knights who crossed the ocean without a ship, armed only with masks and wooden swords.
questions.question: In Puebla and Veracruz, people perform the dance of the Twelve Peers of France. Which emperor did those twelve knights serve?
hints: He ruled a large part of Western Europe.
Among his knights was Roland, hero of a famous medieval epic poem.
He was crowned emperor in the year 800.
questions.fun_fact: The stories of the Twelve Peers reached Mexico in the books of chivalry that the Spanish brought with them.

media.author: Sean Tbear

questions.description: Feathers that have never seen a bird fly up close.

hints: They dance to the beat of a big drum.
You often see them in the Zócalo in Mexico City.
They're also called “Aztec dancers.”
questions.fun_fact: Conchero headdresses often have pheasant or ostrich feathers, which can sway a lot during the dance.

media.author: Jonata Oregón

questions.description: A poetry book that faced the sunrise, and not because the poet was an early bird.

The book collects poems he wrote while he was Mexico's ambassador to India.
It came out the same year humans first walked on the Moon.
questions.fun_fact: Paz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990, the first Mexican ever to receive it.

questions.description: A poet with velvet verses and a sandpaper temper.
questions.question: He was a modernist poet, published “Lascas” in 1901 and was known for picking fights. In what city was Salvador Díaz Mirón born?

His hometown was founded by the Spanish in the 16th century.
It is the most important port in Mexico's history, and it shares its name with its state.
questions.fun_fact: Díaz Mirón spent several years in prison after a fight, and he kept writing poetry there.

hints: The book begins by saying she lived in the north of this town.

Its name starts with T and has three syllables.
questions.fun_fact: “La peor señora del mundo” (The Worst Lady in the World) came out in 1992 and is one of the Mexican children's books most read in schools.

I have two first names, and my last name starts with A.
questions.fun_fact: “El guardagujas” (“The Switchman”) is read as a satire of Mexico's railroads and its red tape.

questions.description: A woman whose life in 1920s Mexico reads like the script of a period telenovela.

questions.fun_fact: Antonieta paid for the Teatro de Ulises, where Xavier Villaurrutia and Salvador Novo acted in and translated avant-garde plays.

questions.description: A stowaway with a fake ID has sneaked onto this bookshelf, and nobody has checked the cover.

hints: Pacheco won the Cervantes Prize in 2009.
The odd one out is a novel written by a woman.
The odd one out was written by Ángeles Mastretta from Puebla.
questions.fun_fact: Pacheco also translated great poets and wrote the column “Inventario” for decades.

media.author: Raul21940

questions.description: An insect that dresses up for a party every day of the year.

hints: I'm a beetle.
I hide my wings under a colorful shell.
My name sounds almost the same as “Catalina.”
questions.fun_fact: A single catarina can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime, which is why gardeners love it so much.

questions.description: A dog so bald it never has to go to the groomer.

hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl.
The Mexica believed it guided souls to Mictlán.
Lots of people lovingly call it “xolo”.
questions.fun_fact: Because it has almost no hair, a xolo's skin feels warm, and people once used it to warm up the sick.

media.author: Yavidaxiu

questions.description: A case of mistaken identity worthy of a telenovela.

It's a close relative of the raccoon.

questions.fun_fact: The American badger sometimes hunts as a team with the coyote: one digs into the burrows and the other catches the prey that runs out.

media.author: Yathin S Krishnappa

questions.description: A bird that never makes it onto the postcards, but works harder than anyone.
questions.question: This black bird has a bald head, circles in the sky looking for dead animals, and its Mexican name comes from Nahuatl. What is it?
hints: It has no feathers on its head so it stays clean while eating.

In English it's called the black vulture.
questions.fun_fact: Its stomach juices are so acidic that they kill germs that would make almost any other animal sick.

questions.question: It's in Campeche, protects Mexico's largest tropical forest and holds an ancient Maya city with huge pyramids. Which reserve is it?
hints: It's a World Heritage Site for both its nature and its history.
Jaguars, pumas and howler monkeys live there.
Its Maya name means “two mounds side by side.”

hints: It eats meat.
Its food has scales.
It even takes on rattlesnakes.

It is the best-known name for the people who founded Tenochtitlan.
Mexico City's most famous stadium has carried the same name for decades.

Without me, fists would go in bare.

To work out how much money each one earns
To choose the color of their gloves
hints: Boxing has strawweight, lightweight, middleweight, heavyweight...
If a boxer comes in too heavy, he can lose the title or pay a fine.
It’s about how many kilos are allowed.
questions.fun_fact: After the weigh-in, many boxers put several kilos back on before stepping into the ring the next day.

It's called “the Pearl of the Pacific.”

Put a superhero’s prefix in front of the old division’s name.

questions.description: An herb so proud of itself that its Spanish name calls it “good.”
questions.question: In Mexico it goes into albóndigas and chicken broth, and its tea is drunk for an upset tummy. What is hierbabuena?
hints: Its leaves are green and smell very fresh.
It's related to the flavor of a lot of chewing gum.
It tastes like the little candies people suck to freshen their breath.
questions.fun_fact: Hierbabuena belongs to the same plant family as oregano, basil and rosemary.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: A question that tastes like the garden and an answer that tastes like an ice-cold pitcher.
questions.question: If someone asks you “¿Qué te pasa, calabaza?”, how does the answer “Nada, nada…” end?
hints: It has to rhyme with “nada”.
It's a cool drink for hot days.
It's made with water, sugar and a sour green fruit.
questions.fun_fact: Squash is native to Mesoamerica and has been grown in Mexico for about 10,000 years.

media.credit: Richard Humphrey · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Richard Humphrey

questions.description: A Cuban star who crossed the Gulf of Mexico to shine in Mexican cinema.
questions.question: I was born in Guanabacoa, Cuba, and was nicknamed “La Única”. In Mexico I played Mercé, the nanny in “Angelitos negros”, with Pedro Infante. Who am I?
hints: I was a singer, pianist and actress.
I was one of the first to record “El manisero” (“The Peanut Vendor”).
My last name sounds a bit like “mountaineer”.
questions.fun_fact: The great Bola de Nieve started his career as her accompanying pianist.

media.credit: Libby norman · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Libby norman

questions.description: A chilango who started in Mexican studios and ended up causing trouble in another galaxy.
questions.question: Which actor, born in Mexico City in 1920, made it big in Hollywood and played Khan, the villain of “Star Trek”?
hints: He made films in Mexico in the 1940s before moving to the United States.
On TV he was the elegant host of “Fantasy Island.”
In “Spy Kids 2” and “Spy Kids 3-D” he played the kids' grandfather.
questions.fun_fact: On “Fantasy Island” he played Mr. Roarke, always dressed in white, for seven seasons.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de

questions.description: Mexico's catchiest song isn't on the radio: it plays down your street at eight o'clock on a Saturday morning.
questions.question: A recording blares down your street: “Se compran colchones, tambores, refrigeradores…” Who is coming by?
questions.answer: The man who buys scrap metal
hints: He isn't coming to sell you anything.
He wants to take away the old things you no longer use.
The recording also offers to buy washing machines, microwaves and anything made of metal you want to sell.
questions.fun_fact: The voice on the most famous recording belongs to María del Mar Terrón, who recorded it as a young girl at her dad's request.

media.credit: Coral2712 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Coral2712

questions.description: Where people argue passionately about who left the trash by the front gate.
questions.question: People gather in the condo courtyard, vote on the maintenance fee and complain about the dog in 3B. What is that meeting called?
hints: There's no piñata and no music.
The people who go live in the same building or on the same street.
Its name says who attends: the people who live next door.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexican condos, the law calls these meetings “asambleas de condóminos,” though everyone just calls them juntas.

media.credit: Lazjak · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lazjak

questions.description: The room with the best view in the house, though nobody brags about it.
questions.question: Many old buildings in Mexico City have small rooms on the rooftop, each with its own bathroom. Who were they built for?
hints: Someone who worked in the building lived there.
That person helped the family with cleaning and cooking.
On the building plans they were called “cuartos de servicio.”
questions.fun_fact: Today many of these rooftop rooms are rented to students or have become small artists' studios.

media.credit: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Case

questions.description: A ring game where everyone spins around until someone ends up facing backward.
questions.question: Finish the children's ring song: “A la rueda, rueda de San Miguel, San Miguel, todos traen su caja de…”
hints: It's something you eat.
It's sweet and sticky.
Bees make it.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the song everyone sings “que se voltee de burro,” and the child named has to turn around and keep playing facing backward.

media.credit: Masmusdjeprat · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Masmusdjeprat

questions.description: It weighs as much as a grade-schooler and always arrives on someone's shoulder.
questions.question: In many Mexican homes, a garrafón like this one is bought every week. What is its water mostly used for?
hints: It's purified water, pricier than tap water.
That's why it isn't wasted on cleaning.
It's the water poured into your glass and used to make meals.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries that drinks the most bottled water per person in the world.

media.credit: MURSHID ELAMARAM · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MURSHID ELAMARAM

questions.description: Where every house is a twin and the guard knows your license plate by heart.
questions.question: Rows of identical houses, a guard booth at the gate and sometimes a shared pool. What is this kind of neighborhood called in Mexico?
hints: It's very common on the edges of cities.
A builder splits a big piece of land into many lots.
Its name comes from dividing something into fractions.
questions.fun_fact: In northern Mexico, many fraccionamientos have English names or names of faraway places, like “Villas de Toscana”.

media.credit: Andre Carrotflower · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andre Carrotflower

questions.description: A dance that needs more ribbons than a sewing shop.
questions.question: It's danced with a huge round headdress of ribbons that spins like a wheel, by Nahua and Totonac dancers, and is famous in Cuetzalan. Which state is it from?
hints: It's danced in a mountain range in east-central Mexico.
This state borders Tlaxcala.
It's the state of mole and Talavera pottery.
questions.fun_fact: The headdress of the Danza de los Quetzales can be more than 1 meter (3 ft) across, and it stands for the sun.

media.credit: MaiWei · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MaiWei

questions.description: A word that smells like fresh salsa and grandma's kitchen.
questions.question: The recipe says: “First, tatema the jitomates and the chiles.” What does tatemar mean?
questions.answer: Roasting them right on the comal or flame until charred
wrong_answers: Boiling them in salted water until they go soft
Grinding them in the molcajete with garlic and onion
Stuffing them with cheese and frying them in egg batter
hints: The word comes from Nahuatl.
Cooks do it to give salsa a smoky flavor.
It happens on the comal or open fire, with no water and no oil.
questions.fun_fact: “Tatemar” comes from the Nahuatl “tlatemati,” and those charred spots are what give salsa its smoky flavor.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: If all its residents stood in line, the line would reach another state.
questions.question: It's Mexico City's most populated borough, home of the Central de Abasto, and its Nahuatl name speaks of stone slabs in the water. Which is it?
hints: It's on the east side of the city.
It has almost 2 million people, more than many Mexican states.
Its name starts with “Izta”, like the volcano Iztaccíhuatl.
questions.fun_fact: Iztapalapa has more people than entire states such as Colima, Campeche or Baja California Sur.

media.credit: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz)

questions.description: Maya scribes had no eraser: every mistake stayed carved in stone forever.
questions.question: You're in Palenque, in front of a stone tablet full of glyphs. About how many different signs does Maya writing have?
hints: It has far more signs than our alphabet.
It combined signs for syllables with signs for whole words.
Several hundred, but fewer than a thousand.
questions.fun_fact: Maya writing could write the same word with a single glyph or spell it out in syllables, like a puzzle.

media.credit: SMU Central University Libraries · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SMU Central University Libraries

questions.description: The family of sauce-covered tortillas has lots of cousins, and all their last names start with “en-.”
questions.question: They're folded tortillas with queso fresco and cream, covered in tomato sauce instead of chile sauce. What is this dish called?
hints: Look closely at what the sauce is made of.
Its name comes from the sauce's main ingredient, not from chile.
Its name hides the Spanish word for tomato.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has a whole family of dishes named this way: enchiladas, enfrijoladas, enmoladas and entomatadas.

media.credit: Armando Gómez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Armando Gómez

questions.description: A tomato that was born to end up in the molcajete.
questions.question: I'm an egg-shaped tomato, firm to the touch and not very juicy; at the market people ask for me for salsas. What am I called?
hints: I'm grown a lot in Sinaloa and in greenhouses all over Mexico.
I'm a favorite for salsa roja and stews.
My name sounds a little French, and a little like salad.
questions.fun_fact: The saladet is one of the most grown tomatoes in Mexico because it holds up well on long trips.

media.credit: jay galvin · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: jay galvin

questions.description: A Latin last name shared by one very spicy family.
questions.question: I'm a Latin name: I group the jalapeño, the habanero and the bell pepper, and Mexico has grown me for thousands of years. Which plant genus am I?
hints: Botanists put all chiles under my name.
I'm not the one for black pepper or the one for onions.
The substance that makes chiles hot is named after me.
questions.fun_fact: Capsaicin, the stuff that makes chiles hot, takes its name from the genus Capsicum.

media.credit: Bhaskaranaidu · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bhaskaranaidu

questions.description: What's left of the elote when there's no elote left.
questions.question: You finish your elote and you're left with the olote, the hard core with no kernels. In the countryside, what has it traditionally been used for?
hints: It has no kernels left, so it's no good for making masa.
Once dry, it becomes light and hard.
It burns well along with firewood.
questions.fun_fact: The word «olote» comes from Nahuatl, just like «elote».

media.credit: Tomascastelazo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tomascastelazo

questions.description: A honey so strange that no bee wants to take the credit.
questions.question: «Miel de agave» is sweet and thick like honey, but it isn't bee honey. Why not?
questions.answer: Because it comes from a plant
wrong_answers: Because it comes from the sea
hints: No animal makes it.
It's harvested in the fields, in places like Jalisco, not in a hive.
It comes from the same plant tequila is made from.
questions.fun_fact: An agave plant can take several years to grow before it's harvested.

media.credit: HOREG Diutey · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: HOREG Diutey

questions.description: A market where they gave you your change in chocolate that wasn't made yet.
questions.question: At a market in Tlaxcala in 1545, a big tomato cost one cacao bean. How many did a guajolota (turkey hen) cost?
hints: A bird is worth much more than a tomato.
But nobody carried giant sacks of cacao to buy food.
It's a round three-digit number.
questions.fun_fact: According to the same price list, a turkey egg was worth three cacao beans.

media.credit: Isai Symens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isai Symens

questions.description: A flower that guards the door better than a watchdog.
questions.question: Take a close look: this plant tastes like anise, and in Morelos people make crosses from its flowers on September 28. What is it called?
hints: Its flowers are small and yellow.
It's a cousin of cempasúchil, but it isn't the Day of the Dead flower.
The crosses go up on the eve of Saint Michael's Day to protect homes and milpas.
questions.fun_fact: Pericón is also called “Mexican tarragon” because it tastes a lot like tarragon.

media.credit: Traper Bemowski · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Traper Bemowski

questions.description: An event where the dress code is a cape and a nice big bunch of rue.
questions.question: Every first Friday in March, I gather on the shore of a lagoon in Veracruz. Curanderos and tourists come for limpias. What am I?
hints: The lagoon is Catemaco, in Los Tuxtlas.
There are limpias, amulets and even a “black mass.”
The people who go there practice magic and sorcery.
questions.fun_fact: The Congreso de Brujos in Catemaco began in 1970, organized by Gonzalo Aguirre, known as the “Brujo Mayor” (Chief Sorcerer).

media.credit: Tobias Maasland · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tobias Maasland

questions.description: Man's best friend… as long as the man gets home early.
questions.question: I'm a huge dog with red eyes. In Chiapas and Central America they say I follow drunks at night, and there's a good white one and a bad black one. Who am I?
hints: I appear on lonely roads late at night.
My white version protects travelers; my black one wants to hurt them.
My name starts with “Ca”.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the legend, the white Cadejo watches over drunks so they get home safe and sound.

media.credit: Famartin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Famartin

questions.description: An actor who worked nights and slept all day, strictly because the role demanded it.
questions.question: Which Spanish-born actor played Count Lavud in the Mexican horror film “El vampiro” (The Vampire, 1957)?
hints: He was almost unknown when he took the role.
He was born in Gijón and moved to Mexico as a young man.
His last name is the Spanish word for oak trees.
questions.fun_fact: Germán Robles was one of the first movie vampires to show fangs, a year before Christopher Lee's British Dracula.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: One night a year when even your grandma wants to see someone fly off the top rope.
questions.question: I left the world's oldest wrestling company in 1992 to start my own, and in 1993 I filled the Plaza de Toros México with the first Triplemanía. Who am I?
hints: He wasn't a star wrestler: he was a promoter who used to work at CMLL.
The company he founded has a name of three identical letters: AAA.
His last name is the Spanish word for a big rock.
questions.fun_fact: About 48,000 people came to the first Triplemanía at the Plaza de Toros México in 1993.

media.credit: Jorge De la Vega · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge De la Vega

questions.description: How to show up at the party as a ring champion without spending a single day at the gym.
questions.question: You're dressing up as a wrestler like El Santo for a party. What do you put on your head to cover your face?
hints: Wrestlers take great care of it.
If they lose it in a bet, everyone sees their face.
It has holes for the eyes and mouth.
questions.fun_fact: For decades, kid-sized wrestling masks have been sold outside Mexican arenas.

media.credit: slgckgc · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: slgckgc

questions.description: Its name already warns you not to try it on your parents' bed.
questions.question: In lucha libre, where does a wrestler dive headfirst when doing a “tope suicida”?
questions.answer: Out of the ring, between the ropes
wrong_answers: Into the center of the mat
Onto the top rope in his corner
hints: He gets a running start inside the ring.
His opponent waits for him down below, close to the crowd.
He goes through the gap between the second and top ropes.
questions.fun_fact: The tope suicida is so risky that the wrestler sometimes ends up landing on the front rows of the crowd.

media.credit: Joe Hernandez joehernandez · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Hernandez joehernandez

questions.description: A school costume with more history than many textbooks.
questions.question: On November 20, many girls dress up as Adelitas, with belts of bullets crossed over their chest. What are those belts called?
hints: They copy what the soldaderas of the Revolution wore.
They were used to carry bullets for the rifle.
Change one letter in “bananas” and you have it.
questions.fun_fact: Many soldaderas of the Revolution didn't just cook and nurse the wounded: they also carried rifles and fought.

media.credit: David Cabrera · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Cabrera

questions.description: A voice that jumps over the fence without asking permission.
questions.question: Falsetto, that leap of the voice up to its highest notes, is the trademark of the huapango and son of one region of Mexico. Which one?
hints: People dance zapateado there on a wooden platform.
It covers parts of San Luis Potosí, Veracruz, Hidalgo and Tamaulipas.
Its son is played with violin, jarana and huapanguera.
questions.fun_fact: Miguel Aceves Mejía was called “the king of falsetto”, even though he was from Chihuahua, far from the Huasteca.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: They don't come to the lienzo charro to watch: they come to steal the show.
questions.question: We ride sidesaddle, in wide skirts and sombreros, and perform figures at a gallop in the lienzo charro. Who are we?
hints: We are the women's event of charrería.
We ride as a team: eight riders who almost brush past each other as we cross.
Our name is also the Spanish word for a skirmish between soldiers.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, UNESCO added charrería to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

media.credit: RubeHM · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: RubeHM

questions.description: A belt that takes itself so seriously it needs weeks to get dressed.
questions.question: Look at this charro piteado belt. What is the shiny thread in its embroidery made of?
hints: It shines a lot, but it isn't metal.
It comes from the leaves of something that grows in the countryside.
It gives the embroidery its name: pita.
questions.fun_fact: Pita is a plant from the pineapple family, and embroidering a good piteado belt can take weeks.

media.credit: Anmuratalla · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Anmuratalla

questions.description: A man who gave bolero its squeakiest little voice… on guitar.
questions.question: In 1944 in New York, I formed one of the most famous bolero trios in the world and gave bolero its small, high-pitched guitar, the requinto. Who am I?
hints: People called me “el Güero.”
My trio was called Los Panchos.
My last name has three letters.
questions.fun_fact: The requinto is smaller than a regular guitar and sounds higher, which makes it perfect for the fancy runs in a bolero.

media.credit: Jo Dusepo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jo Dusepo

questions.description: At a Mexican party, the lungs work harder than the trumpets.
questions.question: You hear it shouted between mariachi songs, at charreadas and at Mexico's national team games. What is “¡ajúa!”?
hints: Nobody gets mad when they hear it.
You often hear it right after a famous line of a ranchera.
It's a cousin of “¡ay, ay, ay!” and “¡viva!”.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexican grito is so loved that many Independence Day parties hold contests to see who can let out the best one.

media.credit: U.S. Air Force AFCENT by Senior Airman Ryan Hayman · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: U.S. Air Force AFCENT by Senior Airman Ryan Hayman

questions.description: Three friends teamed up for a school project, and one got left out.
questions.question: Which of these cities was NOT part of the Triple Alliance that ruled central Mexico before the Spanish Conquest?
hints: Today this city is a borough of Mexico City.
For years the Mexica paid tribute to this Tepanec city.
The alliance was formed precisely to defeat it, in 1428.
questions.fun_fact: Before 1428, the Mexica paid tribute to Azcapotzalco, the very city they later defeated.

media.credit: José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luiz

questions.description: It's made of stone, weighs as much as your backpack and makes the best salsa on the block.
questions.question: How many legs does a molcajete have?
hints: It's carved from volcanic stone and stays steady even on an uneven floor.
It's an odd number.
It's the same number of legs as a camera tripod.
questions.fun_fact: The little stone used to grind in a molcajete is called a tejolote.

media.credit: El Mono Español · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: El Mono Español

questions.description: You walk in for one screw and walk out with half a workshop in a bag.
questions.question: The word “tlapalería” comes from the Nahuatl word “tlapalli.” What does “tlapalli” mean?
hints: At first, these shops mostly sold one kind of thing.
Mexica codices were full of it.
It's what paint has.
questions.fun_fact: Tlapalerías started out selling paints, and over time they filled up with nails, pipes and tools.

media.credit: Daderot · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daderot

questions.description: For the Mexica, gold was nice, but this was the real treasure.
questions.question: The Mexica called it chalchihuitl. It's a green stone, and they valued it more than gold. Which stone is it?
hints: It was made into necklaces, masks and ear ornaments for nobles.
Its color reminded people of water and young corn.
It is also very famous in Chinese art.
questions.fun_fact: When the Spaniards asked for gold, the Mexica were surprised that they didn't value jade as much.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: A horoscope so serious they painted it by hand, with priests as witnesses.
questions.question: The tonalámatl, the Mexica “book of fates,” recorded a ritual calendar. How many days did that calendar have?
hints: It’s shorter than a solar year.
The Maya had a calendar with the same number of days: the tzolkin.
It combines 20 day signs with the numbers 1 to 13.
questions.fun_fact: The 260-day calendar was called the tonalpohualli, and it was used to choose babies’ names.

media.credit: Rosemania · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rosemania

questions.description: An emperor who welcomed some visitors who never left.
questions.question: Which tlatoani ruled Tenochtitlan when Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519?
hints: He was the ninth tlatoani of the Mexica.
Two tlatoanis had his name, and he was the second.
His name lives on in a joke about tourists with an upset stomach.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish he is Moctezuma, in English often Montezuma, but in Nahuatl his name was Motecuhzoma.

media.credit: Steve Cadman from London, U.K. · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steve Cadman from London, U.K.

questions.description: Before becoming king, every tlatoani was just the kid getting scolded at home.
questions.question: Huitzilíhuitl, the second tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, was the son of the first. What was his father's name?
hints: He ruled from the late 14th century.
His name means “handful of reeds.”
His name starts with “A” and ends in “-tli.”
questions.fun_fact: The name Huitzilíhuitl means “hummingbird feather.”

media.credit: Patolocosi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Patolocosi

questions.description: The afternoon the Azteca taught the Brazilians themselves how to samba.
questions.question: You're at Estadio Azteca and El Tri beats Brazil 4–3 in the Confederations Cup final. What year is it?
hints: Cuauhtémoc Blanco was already El Tri's big star.
It was in the 1990s.
It was one year after the 1998 World Cup in France.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first FIFA title ever won by Mexico's senior national team.

media.credit: Carlos Valenzuela Montuy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carlos Valenzuela Montuy

questions.description: A short man who worked miracles in '86, plus a bit of mischief.
questions.question: Which of these has NOTHING to do with Maradona at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico?
hints: Look for the one that happened at a different World Cup.
Two of them were goals against England at the Estadio Azteca.
The odd one out happened in Rio de Janeiro, in 1950.
questions.fun_fact: The “Hand of God” and the “Goal of the Century” came in the same match, just four minutes apart.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A sauna with grass, goalposts and thousands of voices shouting against you.
questions.question: I'm in northern Honduras, I'm the country's biggest stadium, and I made El Tri sweat through qualifiers in the blazing afternoon sun. Which stadium am I?
hints: My city is the industrial capital of Honduras.
I'm not in Tegucigalpa.
I'm in San Pedro Sula.
questions.fun_fact: It opened in 1997 and holds about 37,000 people.

media.credit: TrickyH · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TrickyH

questions.description: The ancient figures that always look good in photos.
questions.question: The clay “caritas sonrientes” (smiling faces) from central Veracruz, in the El Tajín region: from which era are they?
hints: They are from the same time as El Tajín at its peak.
They were made several centuries before the Spanish arrived, but long after the Olmecs.
They are between 1,100 and 1,400 years old.
questions.fun_fact: Many have open mouths and raised arms, as if singing or dancing, and nobody knows for sure why they smile.

media.credit: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium

questions.description: A party where everyone wears the same outfit and nobody gets upset about it.
questions.question: Every March 21, thousands of people dressed in white come to Teotihuacan, stand in front of the Pyramid of the Sun and raise their arms. Why?
questions.answer: To soak up the Sun's energy
hints: Spring begins on that day.
That's why many dress in white and stretch their hands toward the sky.
They believe the Sun “recharges” them like a battery.
questions.fun_fact: This custom of “charging up with energy” is modern: there is no evidence that the people of ancient Teotihuacan ever did it.

media.credit: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Case

questions.description: An ancient culture that ended up with a governor's last name.
questions.question: The Mogollon culture, which influenced Paquimé, is named after some mountains. Where are those mountains?
hints: The mountains carry the last name of an 18th-century Spanish governor.
The Gila River begins in these mountains.
They are in the US state whose capital is Santa Fe.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Ignacio Flores Mogollón governed New Mexico from 1712 to 1715, and his last name ended up naming a mountain range and an entire culture.

media.credit: National Trails Office (US National Park Service) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: National Trails Office (US National Park Service)

questions.description: Some cities are named after saints; this one preferred the garden.
questions.question: The Toltecs called their capital, today's Tula, Hidalgo, Tollan. Which plant does that name come from?
hints: It is a plant that grows in lakes and marshes.
People weave petates (sleeping mats) and chair seats from it.
A famous tree in Oaxaca is named after it.
questions.fun_fact: For the Nahuas, “Tollan” came to mean “great city,” so they also used it for Teotihuacan and Cholula.

media.author: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium

questions.question: At a charreada, they announce that the “floreo de reata” is next. What are you about to see?
questions.answer: A charro doing tricks with a rope
wrong_answers: A charro riding a wild bull
A horse dancing to mariachi music
An escaramuza circling at a gallop
hints: A reata is a rope.
Nobody needs to catch any animal.
He spins the rope in circles and even jumps through them.
questions.fun_fact: The best charros spin the reata both on foot and on horseback, then use the same rope to catch a horse at full gallop.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A field so round that no ball can figure out what it's for.
questions.question: The ruedo of a lienzo charro, the round arena where many of the events take place, is about how many meters across?
hints: Several horses have to fit in it at a gallop.
It's smaller than a soccer field.
It's a little less than half the length of a soccer field.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the ruedo, a lienzo charro has a long lane called the manga, used for events such as the colas, where riders bring down a steer by its tail.

media.credit: IngeRos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: IngeRos

questions.description: A school whose name is so plain that no one would guess it's special.
questions.question: In Mexico, students at an Escuela Normal are called normalistas. What are they training to be?
hints: After they graduate, they work with children and teenagers.
Their training happens in front of a group of students.
Soon they'll be taking attendance and giving homework.
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the French «école normale»: a school that taught the «norm», meaning how to teach.

media.credit: Tomo · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tomo

questions.description: A box with a cross on it that has saved more knees than any superhero.
questions.question: You scrape your knee and open the first aid kit. Before you put on a bandage, what should you do?
questions.answer: Wash it with soap and water
wrong_answers: Put ice on top of it
Pour lots of powder on it
hints: The scrape has dirt and tiny bits of stuff in it.
Germs that cause infections can get into a dirty scrape.
It's the same thing you do to your hands before you eat.
questions.fun_fact: Cleaning a scrape well with water is one of the most important things you can do to stop it from getting infected.

media.credit: Friedrich Haag · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Friedrich Haag

questions.description: A four-legged hero who wore goggles and little boots to work.
questions.question: Frida, the rescue dog, became famous after the 2017 earthquake in Mexico. Which institution did she belong to?
hints: It's part of Mexico's armed forces.
Besides doing rescues, her teammates guard the coasts.
Her human teammates work on ships and in ports.
questions.fun_fact: Before the 2017 earthquake, Frida had already helped with rescues in Haiti and Ecuador.

media.credit: Dktue · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dktue

questions.description: A doctor so important that even the university students had him as their boss.
questions.question: Ignacio Chávez was rector of UNAM, founded a national institute in 1944, and is Mexico's great pioneer in his field. What does that institute treat?
hints: His institute is still running today in the south of Mexico City.
It cares for an organ that works day and night without rest.
Its full name is the Instituto Nacional de Cardiología.
questions.fun_fact: The Instituto Nacional de Cardiología, founded by Ignacio Chávez in 1944, was one of the first hospitals in the world devoted only to the heart.

media.credit: Secretaría de Cultura CDMX · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Secretaría de Cultura CDMX

questions.description: A grandma so famous she's on the box and never gets any older.
questions.question: Chocolate Abuelita comes in round tablets divided into triangles. What is it mainly used to make?
hints: It dissolves in milk or water.
You whip it with a molinillo (wooden whisk) to make it foamy.
It's perfect with a pan de muerto in November.
questions.fun_fact: Chocolate Abuelita is also used to make champurrado, a thick drink made with corn masa.

media.credit: Isai Symens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isai Symens

questions.description: A state named after someone who never, ever gave up.
questions.question: This state is named after an insurgent who went on to become Mexico's second president. Which state is it?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
Its capital is Chilpancingo.
Acapulco and Taxco are there.
questions.fun_fact: Vicente Guerrero and Agustín de Iturbide signed the Plan of Iguala, which led to Mexico winning its independence in 1821.

media.credit: Jorge Mendoza · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Mendoza

questions.description: Its name sounds like a horror movie, but it spends most of the year hiding under a rock.
questions.question: The Sonoran Desert is home to the “Gila monster.” What is it?
hints: It can go months without eating because it stores fat in its tail.
Its skin has black and orange or pink markings.
It's a four-legged reptile, a cousin of Jalisco's “escorpión.”
questions.fun_fact: A diabetes medicine was developed from a substance found in Gila monster saliva.

media.credit: BLMArizona · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: BLMArizona

questions.description: A schoolyard rhyme everyone knows by heart and nobody learned in class.
questions.question: A children's rhyme starts with “De tin marín, de do pingüé” and goes on with “cúcara, mácara”. What are those words?
hints: Kids pass it down from one generation to the next, no book needed.
Every country, even every neighborhood, says it a little differently.
Nobody knows what they mean, because they don't mean anything.
questions.fun_fact: The rhyme ends with “títere fue”, and many families add “yo no fui, fue Teté” to stretch out the luck.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: On the highway, sometimes one hand is enough to chat with every car.
questions.question: Look at the photo: in Mexico, why is this person by the side of the road holding up a thumb?
wrong_answers: To signal that the car is full
To ask drivers to slow down
hints: People use this gesture on roads all over the world.
This person doesn't have their own car for this trip.
It's the Mexican word for when someone gives you a free ride in their car.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico people also say “dar raite,” from the English word “ride,” when someone gives you a lift.

media.credit: Eli Duke from Portland, OR, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eli Duke from Portland, OR, USA

questions.description: A doctor who never writes you a prescription but dances better than your uncles at parties.
questions.question: He has a big mustache, wears a white coat, dances outside drugstores, and fans throw plush toys of him at singers at concerts. Which chain is he the mascot of?
hints: It's one of the biggest drugstore chains in Mexico.
The chain sells generic medicines at low prices.
The mascot is called Doctor Simi.
questions.fun_fact: The Doctor Simi character is based on Víctor González Torres, the founder of Farmacias Similares.

media.credit: Zalasem1 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zalasem1

questions.description: In August, with back-to-school season, the papelería gets more packed than the Metro at rush hour.
questions.question: At the papelería, you ask for “a dozen” pencils. How many pencils do you get?
hints: It's more than ten.
Eggs are often sold this way too, in cartons.
It's the number of months in a year.
questions.fun_fact: Half a dozen is 6, and a dozen dozens, 144, is called a gross.

media.credit: SpiritedMichelle · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SpiritedMichelle

questions.description: It shows up with a siren, flashing lights and in a big hurry, but never to a party.
questions.question: Look at this Cruz Roja Mexicana vehicle. Who works on board to help people?
hints: They know first aid.
They carry bandages, oxygen and a stretcher.
Their job is a lot like a nurse's, but out on the street.
questions.fun_fact: The Cruz Roja Mexicana was founded in 1910, and every year it collects money in the streets to pay for its ambulances.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: He walks more than anyone in the colonia and always has something for you.
questions.question: Look at this worker. What does he deliver to people's homes?
hints: He carries a big bag over his shoulder.
What he brings sometimes has stamps stuck on it.
He works for the post office.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, Mail Carrier Day (Día del Cartero) is celebrated on November 12.

media.credit: John Charlton · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Charlton

questions.description: Mexican schools have clothes for every occasion, except one.
questions.question: Many schools in Mexico have several uniforms. Which of these does NOT normally exist?
hints: Three of them are worn at school.
One is for ceremonies and another for P.E.
Picture going to class in a swimsuit.
questions.fun_fact: The dress uniform (uniforme de gala) usually has a white shirt and is worn for ceremonies and the Monday flag salute.

media.credit: GeorgeLouis · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: GeorgeLouis

questions.description: Eleven numbers that follow you from your first job all the way to retirement.
questions.question: It's an 11-digit number: you need it for your first formal job and to go to your family clinic. Which institution gives it to you?
hints: It has nothing to do with voting or taxes.
It has clinics and hospitals all over the country.
People call it “el Seguro.”
questions.fun_fact: The IMSS was founded in 1943 and is one of the largest health institutions in Latin America.

media.credit: Harrison Keely · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Harrison Keely

questions.description: Suddenly the whole colonia goes dark and someone yells “¡Se fue la luz!”
questions.question: There's a blackout: no TV, the fridge isn't cooling and the lights won't turn on. What can you still use to cook?
hints: Think about how food gets heated in your home.
It runs on a tank or a pipe.
You can light it with a match.
questions.fun_fact: Stoves with electric ignition can still be lit with a match when the power goes out.

media.credit: Akkbula · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Akkbula

questions.description: The recess bell rings and half the school runs to the same place.
questions.question: I open at recess, sell tortas, chips with salsa and aguas frescas, and always have a line. What am I?
hints: You don't get sent here for misbehaving.
You need a few coins.
Many people call it “la cooperativa”.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican schools the snack shop (la tiendita) is called the “cooperativa” because school co-ops of students, parents and teachers were set up to run it.

media.credit: Jack Corn · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jack Corn

questions.description: The Poli has lots of schools, but one snuck in from the rival university.
questions.question: Which of these schools does NOT belong to the IPN?
hints: Three of them belong to the Poli, whose mascot is a white donkey.
The odd one out is at the same level as a prepa.
It belongs to the university of the Pumas.
questions.fun_fact: The IPN was founded in 1936, while Lázaro Cárdenas was president.

media.credit: Jezuzz.hdz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jezuzz.hdz

questions.description: A pineapple riding shotgun and meat spinning like a fair ride.
questions.question: Look at the photo: who brought this way of roasting meat on a vertical spit, the trompo, to Mexico?
hints: They arrived in Mexico in the early 20th century, mostly in Puebla.
In their homeland, this meat is traditionally made with lamb, not pork.
Puebla still sells tacos árabes, cousins of tacos al pastor.
questions.fun_fact: Tacos al pastor were born when Mexican taco makers swapped the lamb of shawarma for pork marinated in chile and topped it with pineapple.

media.credit: Eduardo Francisco Vazquez Murillo · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eduardo Francisco Vazquez Murillo

questions.description: The Maya had no cell phones, but they never forgot a birthday.
questions.question: The Maya solar calendar, the Haab, had 18 months of 20 days each, plus a few extra days at the end. How many days did it have in total?
hints: It followed the journey of the Sun, just like our calendar.
The extra days were very few, and the Maya thought they were unlucky.
It’s the same number of days as a normal year.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya also had a sacred calendar, the Tzolkin, of 260 days, and they used it together with the Haab.

media.credit: Eric Polk · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eric Polk

questions.description: A snack with a passport from one side of the world and a birth certificate from the other.
questions.question: Cacahuates japoneses (“Japanese peanuts”) were invented in Mexico City. Why are they called “Japanese”?
questions.answer: Their inventor was a Japanese immigrant
wrong_answers: A Japanese emperor once tasted them
A Tokyo chef used to sell them
hints: Their inventor arrived in Mexico before World War II.
He started out selling them at the La Merced market.
His last name was Nakatani, and he founded the Nipón brand.
questions.fun_fact: Yoshigei Nakatani based the crunchy coating on a snack from his homeland, yet in Japan almost nobody knows “Japanese” peanuts.

media.credit: Gogerr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gogerr

questions.description: A museum where not touching anything is against the rules.
questions.question: In which city is El Trompo, the interactive science and technology museum?
hints: The city is in the north of the country.
It sits right on the border with the United States.
It is the largest city in Baja California.
questions.fun_fact: El Trompo in Tijuana opened in 2008, and its name honors the traditional Mexican spinning top.

media.credit: Zmpzst · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zmpzst

questions.description: At the tiendita on the corner, there are always more cravings than coins in your pocket.
questions.question: It's round, made of peanuts, crumbles very easily, and its wrapper has a red rose on it. Which candy is it?
hints: You can buy it at any tiendita, and it falls out of piñatas.
It's a Mexican childhood classic, and each one comes wrapped in cellophane.
Its most famous brand is De la Rosa, from Guadalajara.
questions.fun_fact: There's a famous trick for opening a mazapán without breaking it: squeeze it a little before you take off the wrapper.

media.credit: Natalia Wilson · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Natalia Wilson

questions.description: Some college students' homework that ended up being turned in from orbit.
questions.question: Students at UPAEP in Puebla built it with NASA's help; it flew on a SpaceX rocket in 2019 and was released from the International Space Station. Which satellite was it?
hints: It's a tiny satellite, the kind called a CubeSat.
It was the first Mexican satellite launched into space from the International Space Station.
Its name plays on the people who founded Tenochtitlan and the word “technology.”
questions.fun_fact: AztechSat-1 is about 10 centimeters (4 inches) on each side and weighs just over 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds).

media.credit: NASA · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NASA

questions.description: A dish that gets “cooked” with no stove, no oven and not a single match.
questions.question: Look at the state highlighted on the map: aguachile, raw shrimp soaked in lime juice and chili, comes from here. Which state is it?
hints: It's on the Pacific coast.
It's famous for its banda music with the tambora drum.
The port of Mazatlán is there.
questions.fun_fact: The original aguachile is thought to have had no shrimp at all, just dried meat with water and chiltepín chili.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: A dance that needs no dance floor, just a tall pole and nerves of steel.
questions.question: You're in Papantla watching the voladores: four men spin down upside down, and each one makes 13 turns. How many turns is that in total?
hints: You need to multiply.
There are four voladores, and each one makes the same number of turns.
It's the same as 4 × 13.
questions.fun_fact: The 52 turns stand for the 52 years of one cycle of the Mesoamerican calendar.

media.credit: Larry D. Moore · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Larry D. Moore

questions.description: A city where the jacket and the swimsuit fight over space in your suitcase.
questions.question: Cuernavaca is “the City of Eternal Spring.” Roughly how high above sea level is it?
hints: It's not on the coast.
Its mild climate comes from sitting in a valley between mountains, south of Mexico City.
It's lower than Mexico City, which is at about 2,240 m (7,350 ft), but still far above the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its mild weather all year, both Hernán Cortés and Emperor Maximilian had vacation homes in Cuernavaca.

media.credit: Zoran Lazic · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zoran Lazic

questions.description: A snack so spicy that even the bag asks for a glass of water.
questions.question: It's a seed with a thin red skin, coated in chile powder and sold in little bags at the corner store. What is this snack called?
hints: People eat it a lot at the movies, at the stadium and with lime.
The seed inside is also turned into a spread for bread.
Unlike the Japanese-style ones, it has no flour crust.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico peanuts are called cacahuates, from the Nahuatl word tlalcacáhuatl, “cacao of the earth.”

media.credit: Adam Jones · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Jones

questions.description: A fruit with an Arabic passport and a chili-covered Mexican soul.
questions.question: My name comes from Arabic and means “date of India.” In Mexico I'm drunk as a brown agua fresca and coated in chili in candies. What am I?
hints: My flavor is sweet and sour.
I grow in hard-shelled pods.
My pulp is brown and sticky, with shiny seeds.
questions.fun_fact: Tamarind is native to Africa, but it has been part of Mexican food since colonial times.

media.credit: Gzzz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gzzz

questions.description: An open-air gym where everyone is dressed up as a giant cat.
questions.question: Every May in Zitlala, Guerrero, men in tiger masks face off in ritual fights. It's a very old custom. According to tradition, why do they do it?
questions.answer: To ask for rain for the milpas
wrong_answers: To celebrate the end of the harvest
To remember a battle against the Spanish
hints: May comes right before planting season starts.
It has to do with the sky and the fields.
The farmers hope water will soon fall from the sky.
questions.fun_fact: Zitlala's tiger masks are made of hardened leather and sometimes have whiskers made of real bristles.

media.credit: পাপৰি বৰা · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: পাপৰি বৰা

questions.description: A party where one person wears more dress than all the guests put together.
questions.question: I arrive at the party dressed like a princess, turn a very special age and open the dancing with a waltz. Who am I?
hints: The party usually has a big hall, a cake and lots of family.
Many girls in Mexico dream of this party for years.
I'm not a little girl anymore: I'm turning fifteen.
questions.fun_fact: At many XV años parties, the birthday girl is given her “last doll” as a farewell to childhood.

media.author: Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums

questions.description: Dancers so eager you can hear their rattles from the next block over.
questions.question: In Saltillo, Chihuahua and other northern cities, hundreds of matachines groups dance each year at their biggest fiesta. On what date is it?
hints: It's a religious holiday, not a patriotic one.
It's the day of Mexico's most beloved Virgin.
Many groups dance in front of the Basilica in Mexico City.
questions.fun_fact: The matachines dance for the Virgin of Guadalupe wearing headdresses and colorful fringed costumes, and shaking rattles.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: Dancers with wigs so fluffy they look fresh out of the dryer.
questions.question: These dancers are part of a January fiesta listed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Which state are they from?
hints: It's a state in southeastern Mexico.
They're called parachicos and wear wooden masks and carry rattles.
Its capital is Tuxtla Gutiérrez.
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO added the Fiesta Grande of January in Chiapa de Corzo to its list in 2010.

media.credit: Alonso Cerro · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alonso Cerro

questions.description: In Mexico this X and O game is called “gato”, but no cat ever gets hurt.
questions.question: Look at this gato (tic-tac-toe) board. How many squares does it have for your X's and O's?
hints: Count the little squares slowly.
It has three rows.
Each row has three squares: 3 + 3 + 3.
questions.fun_fact: If neither player ever makes a mistake, a game of gato always ends in a tie.

media.author: Sfieldman

questions.description: Streets numbered like a grocery list: Eje 1, Eje 2, Eje 3… and the traffic is just as bad.
questions.question: In which decade were the ejes viales built, the big avenues that cross Mexico City from side to side?
hints: It was before the Metrobús existed.
They were built under city regent Carlos Hank González.
They opened in 1979, while José López Portillo was president.
questions.fun_fact: To open the ejes viales, thousands of houses and trees were torn down in a very short time.

questions.description: Miss it and you'll get to school late and in a big hurry.
questions.question: It carries lots of seated people, has a driver and stops at corners to let people on. In Mexico they call it a camión. What is it?
hints: It travels on the street, not on rails or through the air.
It has a bell you ring to ask to get off.
In other Spanish-speaking countries it's called a «colectivo» or a «guagua».
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, «camión» can mean a passenger bus or a cargo truck; it all depends on the conversation.

His first names are the Spanish form of the Roman general who loved Cleopatra.

Javier Alatorre has hosted it for many years.

questions.description: Four spinning chairs, lots of drama and a red button everyone wants to press.

questions.description: A family of orange snacks finds out there's an impostor at the reunion.

Nearby is Wirikuta, the sacred desert that the Wixárika (Huichol) people travel to on pilgrimage.
It's the same state as the surrealist garden of Xilitla and the red enchiladas filled with cheese.
questions.fun_fact: Scenes from the movie “The Mexican” (2001), with Brad Pitt and Julia Roberts, were filmed in Real de Catorce.

questions.description: A boat ride with mariachis, elotes and zero seasickness… well, almost.
questions.question: Venice is to gondolas as Xochimilco is to…
hints: They are flat boats pushed along with a long pole.

Their name starts with “Tra-.”
questions.fun_fact: Every trajinera has its name painted on its arch, and many have women's names, like “Lupita” or “Rosita.”

questions.description: If comic characters could talk out loud, they wouldn't need it.
questions.question: Fill in the blank: in comics, the words the characters say are written inside a speech ___.
hints: It has a little tail pointing at whoever is talking.
When a character is thinking, it's drawn like a cloud.
It shares its name with something you blow up at parties.
questions.fun_fact: When a character shouts, the balloon is often drawn with spikes, like an explosion.

questions.description: A government inspector arrives in a small town, and nobody knows whether to laugh or hide.
questions.question: In which year was “Calzonzin Inspector” released, Alfonso Arau's film based on Rius's “Los Supermachos”?
hints: The comic it is based on started in the mid-1960s.
It came out in the same decade that El Chavo del Ocho became famous.
It was in the mid-1970s.
questions.fun_fact: Alfonso Arau, the film's director, later also directed “Like Water for Chocolate”.

media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: In a town where the powerful think they're very smart, there's always someone smarter.
questions.question: In Rius's comic “Los Supermachos”, who is the clever Indigenous man from San Garabato who makes fun of the authorities?
hints: He is the main character of the comic.
His name recalls an ancient Purépecha ruler.
His surname also appears in the title of a film by Alfonso Arau.
questions.fun_fact: The name Calzonzin recalls Tangáxoan Calzontzin, the last great lord of the Purépecha people.

media.author: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico

questions.description: Comics live in little rectangular apartments, one next to the other.
questions.question: It's each of the boxes in a comic: it has a border, and inside go the drawings and speech bubbles. What is it called?
hints: A comic book page usually has several of them.
The white space between them is called the “gutter”.
It's the same word as a flat section of a door, or a group of experts on stage.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish a panel is a “viñeta”, from “viña” (vineyard): in old books, viñetas were ornaments of grape leaves and bunches, the same root as the English “vignette”.

questions.description: Art with dual citizenship, long before passports existed.
questions.question: José Moreno Villa called the art carved by Indigenous hands in the 16th century “tequitqui”, Nahuatl for “tributary”. Where is it mostly found?
hints: It mixes European symbols with pre-Hispanic forms.
You can see it on stone crosses, church doorways and chapels.
The builders were the same people who were bringing Christianity to the towns.
questions.fun_fact: Some tequitqui atrium crosses have a piece of obsidian at the center, like the ancient sacred mirrors.

questions.description: A balcony with a bigger crowd than any concert of the year.
questions.question: Look at this palace on the Zócalo, where the viceroys once lived. What happens on its central balcony every September 15?
hints: It's a national holiday.
A bell rings and the flag is waved.
At the end everyone shouts “¡Viva México!”
questions.fun_fact: Above the central balcony hangs the bell that Miguel Hidalgo rang in Dolores in 1810.

media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: The letters on the movie listings have their own school rules too.
questions.question: Under Mexico's movie ratings, an AA film is understandable for children under what age?
hints: The B rating is already for teens aged 12 and up.
It's fewer than the fingers on two hands.
It's a typical age for a kid in second grade.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, an A rating means the film is for all audiences, while AA also signals that it is made to appeal to the youngest viewers.

media.author: Jeff Gunn from Atlanta, USA

questions.question: The Guadalajara Film Festival, which gives out the Mayahuel Award, started as a showcase of Mexican cinema. In which decade?
hints: It's older than the “new Mexican cinema” of the nineties.
It started the same year Mexico hosted its second soccer World Cup.
It was 1986.
questions.fun_fact: Today the Guadalajara Film Festival is one of the most important in Latin America, and its trophy honors Mayahuel, the Aztec goddess of the maguey.

questions.description: A voice so powerful it could turn its own hair gold.
questions.question: You're watching “Dragon Ball Z” on TV and Goku shouts with Mario Castañeda's voice. In which decade did he start dubbing adult Goku?
hints: It was before phones could go online.
The series premiered in Japan in 1989; the Spanish dub came later.
It was the same decade the Nintendo 64 came out.
questions.fun_fact: Mario Castañeda is also the Spanish voice of Bruce Willis in many of his movies.

questions.description: The laziest cat in the alley finally landed a gig on the big screen.
questions.question: In what year did “Don Gato y su pandilla” (Top Cat: The Movie), the Mexican-made animated film about the famous alley cat, come out?
hints: It was already the 21st century.
It came out the same year as “La leyenda de la Llorona”.
It was early in the 2010s.
questions.fun_fact: The film was made by the Mexican studio Ánima, and in Mexico the Don Gato cartoon is so loved that he almost became a national character.

questions.description: A thief who becomes a teacher: every principal's worst nightmare.
questions.question: In which year did “No Manches Frida,” the school comedy with Omar Chaparro and Martha Higareda, come out?
hints: It's from the second half of the 2010s.
Its sequel came out in 2019.
It was the year of the Rio de Janeiro Olympics.
questions.fun_fact: “No Manches Frida” is the Mexican version of the German comedy “Fack ju Göhte.”

questions.description: You can't go to the movies in pajamas, but here it almost feels like your own living room.
questions.question: You're in a Cinépolis VIP theater. Which of these is NOT part of the experience?
questions.answer: Seats that move and splash you with water
wrong_answers: A waiter who brings you your food
A menu of dishes and drinks
hints: The VIP theater is about being comfortable and relaxed.
There they spoil you with food, not with scares.
Moving and getting wet belongs to another kind of theater, more adventure than rest.
questions.fun_fact: Cinépolis was born in Morelia, Michoacán, and today has theaters in many countries, including India.

A small stick and a spool
hints: You play it sitting on the floor.
You go up round by round: first you pick up one at a time, then two at a time…
The pieces look like little metal or plastic stars.
questions.fun_fact: Long before metal pieces, matatena was played with pebbles, seeds or little bones.
